Section 16 · Anemia pharmacology

Iron, Vitamins, Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents and the Hemoglobinopathy Drugs

Machine 1, the erythron. Every drug here answers one question: which ingredient is missing? Iron, vitamin B12, folate, or the erythropoietin signal itself.

Abbreviations used in this section OTC over the counter · PPI proton pump inhibitor · H2RA histamine-2 receptor antagonist · IV intravenous · IM intramuscular · FGF23 fibroblast growth factor 23 — a hormone that makes the kidney dump phosphate · NYHA New York Heart Association heart failure classes · HFrEF heart failure with reduced ejection fraction · DHFR dihydrofolate reductase — the enzyme that activates folic acid · ESA erythropoiesis-stimulating agent · HIF-PHI hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor · G-CSF granulocyte colony-stimulating factor · PNH paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

Oral iron — the cheapest drug on the list and the one patients quit

🔑 One fact drives every rule

Only ferrous (Fe²⁺) iron crosses the gut wall, and only in an acidic duodenum. Everything that raises stomach pH or holds iron in the wrong oxidation state is a failure mode.

  • Dosing: classic adult target 150–200 mg elemental iron daily. Newer data favour alternate-day dosing — each dose spikes hepcidin for roughly a day, so a second dose runs into a closed door.
  • Timing: at least 1 hour before meals; but giving it with food is an acceptable trade when that is the only way the patient will take it. An absorbed smaller dose beats a refused larger one.
  • Formulations to avoid: enteric-coated and sustained-release — they release iron distal to the duodenum, past the absorption window.
  • Best dietary sources: meat, fish and poultry (heme iron). Milk and tea reduce absorption.
Salt (typical tablet)Elemental iron per tabletPractical note
ferrous sulfate 325 mg~65 mgThe default. Cheapest, best studied, most gastrointestinal complaints
ferrous gluconate 325 mg~36 mgLess elemental iron per pill → often better tolerated, but you need more pills
ferrous fumarate 325 mg~106 mgMost concentrated — fewest tablets, most upset
ferric maltol30 mg twice dailyNot an iron salt — iron is absorbed off the maltol molecule, so it avoids the salt-driven intolerance that wrecks adherence
🪝 Memory hook — “Fe²⁺ = Free to enter”

Fe2+ (ferrous) = the “2” that gets through the door. Fe³⁺ (ferric) must be reduced first — vitamin C is the reducing agent, dropping the pH and converting Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺. And: “E-C and S-R are D-O-A” — Enteric-Coated and Sustained-Release arrive Dead On Arrival, downstream of the absorption window.

⚠️ Adverse effects of oral iron — the real reason therapy fails ★ HY

Gastrointestinal effects are extremely common: metallic taste, nausea, flatulence, constipation, diarrhea, epigastric distress, vomiting. Patients are also bothered by itching and by black/green or tarry stools that stain clothing and cause alarm about bleeding. The result is poor adherence — the single most common reason a “treatment failure” is not a treatment failure at all.

Interactions: antacids, H2 receptor blockers and proton pump inhibitors all raise gastric pH and impair absorption — separate them by iron 2 hours before, or 4 hours after, an antacid.

🩺 When to give up on the oral route ★ HY

Switch to parenteral iron for: iron malabsorption · intolerance of oral iron · nonadherence · severe or ongoing blood loss (losing it faster than the gut can absorb) · gastric surgery (less acid, bypassed duodenum) · malabsorption syndromes (celiac, Whipple, bacterial overgrowth).

Knowing it worked: a reticulocyte bump at 7–10 days and a hemoglobin rise of roughly 1 g/dL every 2–3 weeks. Then keep going — continue iron for 3–6 months after the hemoglobin normalizes to refill ferritin. Stopping when the hemoglobin looks pretty is the classic under-treatment.

Intravenous iron — and the acute toxicity question

🔑 Every IV iron product, same three rules
  • Administer slowly at first and observe for infusion reactions.
  • Non-allergic infusion reactions are common and self-limiting: urticaria, palpitations, dizziness, and neck and back spasm. This is not anaphylaxis — recognizing the difference prevents needlessly labelling a patient iron-allergic for life.
  • True adverse effects: allergic reactions including life-threatening anaphylaxis (exceedingly rare), hypotension, dizziness, dyspnea, headache, lower back pain, arthralgia, syncope. Many are minimized by decreasing the dose or the rate.
  • Premedication for asthma or more than one drug allergy: methylprednisolone 125 mg IV.
⚠️ Do NOT premedicate with diphenhydramine ★ HY

Counterintuitive and heavily testable. Diphenhydramine does not prevent the reaction and causes its own: hypotension, somnolence, flushing, dizziness, irritability, nasal congestion, wheezing and supraventricular tachycardia — a list that looks exactly like the infusion reaction you were trying to prevent, which then gets misattributed to the iron. Steroid yes, Benadryl no.

DrugWhat makes it different
ferric carboxymaltoseTwo flagship facts: causes hypophosphatemia that may be SEVERE (it raises FGF23, increasing urinary phosphate excretion), and is approved in heart failure
iron sucroseWorkhorse in dialysis units; small repeated doses, long safety record
sodium ferric gluconateAlso a small-dose, repeated-infusion product
ferumoxytolLarge dose in few visits; it is an iron oxide, so it can interfere with magnetic resonance imaging for up to ~3 months
ferric derisomaltoseTotal replacement in a single visit; notably less hypophosphatemia than ferric carboxymaltose
low-molecular-weight iron dextranThe dextran carrying the historical anaphylaxis reputation — a test dose is the tradition here
🩺 Iron as a heart failure drug

Ferric carboxymaltose is approved for NYHA class II/III heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and iron deficiency, with or without anemia, to improve exercise capacity. Iron deficiency is present in roughly 30% of heart failure patients. Note the striking part: the patient does not have to be anemic — this is treating the iron-starved myocyte, not the hemoglobin.

🪝 Memory hook — “CarboxyMaltose Munches Phosphate”

Carboxymaltose → Crashes phosphate (via FGF23), and Cardiac indication (heart failure). Three C's, one drug.

Iron toxicity and overload — the reversal agents ★ HY

☠️

Acute iron toxicity

Classically an accidental pediatric ingestion of adult iron tablets — iron is one of the leading causes of poisoning death in young children.

The antidote is deferoxamine, given parenterally, which chelates free iron and is excreted in the urine (classically turning it a reddish “vin rosé” colour). Supportive care and, in massive ingestion, whole bowel irrigation accompany it.

🔗

Chronic iron overload

The consequence of a lifelong transfusion programme — thalassemia major, chronically transfused sickle cell disease. There is no physiologic route to excrete iron, so it accumulates in heart, liver and endocrine organs.

Removed pharmacologically with an oral or parenteral chelator, chosen largely by tolerability and boxed warning — see the table.

ChelatorRouteSignature problem
deferasiroxOral, once dailyBoxed warning: renal failure, hepatic failure, gastrointestinal hemorrhage
deferiproneOral, three times dailyBoxed warning: agranulocytosis / neutropenia — weekly white cell counts
deferoxamineParenteralThe burden is the problem: 8–12 hour subcutaneous infusions; also ocular and auditory toxicity. This is also the acute-toxicity antidote
🪝 Memory hook — the three chelators, by mouth-count

Deferasirox = once a day, oral. Deferiprone = three times a day, oral, and it robs your neutrophils. Deferoxamine = the old one, under the skin all night. Convenience improved with each generation; the boxed warnings changed shape but never went away.

Vitamin B12 and folate as drugs

Cyanocobalamin

vitamin B12 replacement

Available OTC (multivitamins, B-complex) and by prescription as oral, intranasal and injectable (IM and subcutaneous). The injectable and intranasal routes bypass a broken gut entirely — essential in pernicious anemia. Adverse effects are rare; the two uncommon ones both come from suddenly restarting a stalled marrow: hypokalemia (potassium pulled into new cells) and hyperuricemia (nucleic acid turnover).

Folic acid

vitamin B9 replacement

1 mg daily is standard replacement; 1–5 mg in malabsorption; 500 micrograms for anticonvulsant-induced megaloblastic anemia, so the anticonvulsant need not be stopped. Nontoxic even at high doses — rapidly excreted in urine. Long-term dosing in chronic hemolysis, pregnancy and dialysis.

Folinic acid (leucovorin)

the rescue agent

Bypasses the DHFR step and is directly converted to active folate forms. Methotrexate inhibits DHFR, so in a methotrexate-poisoned patient giving folic acid is useless — the enzyme that would activate it is exactly the one blocked. Folinic acid is already past that step.

🪝 Memory hooks for the vitamins

“FoliNic is fiNished” — N for “No enzyme needed”. Folic acid still needs DHFR, which methotrexate has already broken. “MetForMin and the PPI Pinch B12” — metformin pinches it at the ileum (calcium-dependent uptake at the end of the tube), the proton pump inhibitor pinches it at the stomach (no acid, no release from food). And: “B12 fixes the nerves; folate only fixes the numbers.”

Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents ★ HY

🔑 The class, fully specified — this objective asks for all of it
  • The agents: recombinant epoetin alfa and darbepoetin alfa. Same mechanism; darbepoetin has a longer half-life and is dosed less frequently. Methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta is the longest-acting.
  • Mechanism of action: stimulate the division and differentiation of committed erythroid progenitor cells, and induce release of reticulocytes from the marrow into the blood, where they mature. There is a dose–response relationship: the reticulocyte count rises first, then hematocrit and hemoglobin.
  • Route: all may be given IV or subcutaneously. Subcutaneous epoetin has a prolonged absorption phase → extended half-life → target hemoglobin maintained at doses 15–30% lower than IV.
  • Approved indications: anemia of chronic kidney disease and anemia due to chemotherapy in cancer patients. Sometimes used in anemia of inflammation, but not FDA-approved for it.
  • When to initiate: only when the anemia is symptomatic and the goal is avoiding transfusion — and only after iron stores are checked and repleted. Not for acute correction of severe anemia; erythropoiesis is delayed in onset and an ESA is not a substitute for emergency transfusion.
  • Pregnancy: use only when clearly needed; safety is not established, and the thrombotic risk of the class is a concern.
⚠️ The four US boxed warnings — they share one sentence ★ HY

Every one of them ends in “use the lowest dose needed to avoid transfusion.”

  1. Cardiovascular events. Increased serious cardiovascular events, myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism, vascular access thrombosis and death when targeting hemoglobin above 11 g/dL — with no additional benefit there.
  2. Cancer patients. Shortened overall survival and/or increased tumour progression or recurrence in breast, cervical, head and neck, lymphoid and non-small cell lung cancer. Use in cancer only for anemia from concurrent myelosuppressive chemotherapy, discontinue when the chemotherapy course finishes, and do not use when the anticipated outcome is curative.
  3. Chronic kidney disease patients. Increased death, serious cardiovascular events and stroke when targeting hemoglobin above 11 g/dL.
  4. Perisurgery patients. Increased deep venous thrombosis in orthopaedic surgery. DVT prophylaxis is strongly recommended whenever ESAs are used to reduce transfusions in surgical patients.
Warning / precautionWhat to do about it
Hypertension — the most common adverse effect, in up to one third of treated patientsCaution with a history of hypertension; contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension. Decrease the dose if hemoglobin rises more than 1 g/dL in any 2-week period. Control blood pressure before starting. Hypertensive encephalopathy has been reported. Less blood pressure rise when given subcutaneously
SeizuresRisk increased with epoetin alfa in chronic kidney disease; monitor for neurologic symptoms during the first several months
Severe anemia or acute blood lossOnset is delayed — not a substitute for emergency transfusion
Other adverse effectsNausea, headache, fever, bone pain, fatigue. Less common: seizures, thrombotic events, rash and injection-site reactions
🪝 Memory hook — “Eleven is the ceiling”

Every ESA boxed warning turns on the same number: hemoglobin above 11 g/dL = harm with no benefit. And the rate rule rides alongside it: more than 1 g/dL in 2 weeks = cut the dose. Two numbers — 11, and 1-in-2 — cover most of what gets asked. Think of an ESA as a thermostat set to “just warm enough not to transfuse”, never to “comfortable”.

🩺 Iron first, signal second

An ESA drives the marrow to build red cells, and building red cells consumes iron fast. Give an ESA to an iron-deplete patient and you create functional iron deficiency: the order is shouted, the factory has no raw material, and the hemoglobin does not move. Check and replete iron before blaming the ESA for not working — this is the most common reason for apparent ESA resistance.

🧠 The newer class — HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors

Vadadustat (daprodustat was withdrawn from the US market in late 2024 for commercial, not safety, reasons). Mechanism: HIF is a key regulator of the erythropoietin gene; normally prolyl hydroxylases tag HIF for destruction whenever oxygen is plentiful. Inhibiting them raises intracellular HIF, activates the oxygen-sensing pathway and stimulates erythropoiesis — it convinces the cell it is at altitude. Oral, for anemia of chronic kidney disease in adults on dialysis ≥ 3 months; the oral route is the entire selling point against injected ESAs.

Boxed warning for increased thrombotic events. Contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, and in acute coronary syndrome or cerebrovascular events within 3 months. Caution in malignancy — the pathway can stimulate cancer growth. Memory hook: fake altitude in a pill — which also tells you the side effects: everything a body at altitude with thicker blood gets, hypertension and clots.

Hemoglobinopathy drugs, growth factors and the bleeding-disorder therapeutics

Hydroxyurea

fetal hemoglobin inducer · sickle cell

An antineoplastic agent moonlighting as a sickle cell drug — which is the whole side-effect profile in one line. Raises HbF (threshold to remember: HbF ≥ 20% reduces acute complications). Also raises nitric oxide, reduces neutrophils and monocytes, increases red cell deformability, decreases adhesion to endothelium. Start 15 mg/kg once daily. Two boxed warnings: severe myelosuppression, and carcinogenicity. Also dry skin and nail hyperpigmentation.

Luspatercept

erythroid maturation agent · beta thalassemia, low-risk MDS

Helps late-stage red cells develop normally — it unblocks the final step of the assembly line. Not a growth signal like an ESA, which matters because thalassemia's problem is ineffective erythropoiesis: an ESA would only shout louder at a line already jammed at the end.

Mitapivat

pyruvate kinase activator · oral

The first oral pill for alpha- and beta-thalassemia anemia; also approved for pyruvate kinase deficiency. Increases cellular energy, keeping red cells alive longer. Interaction trap: a substrate and a broad inducer of CYP3A4, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19 and UGT1A1 — it can lower levels of many co-prescribed drugs, oral contraceptives among them.

Filgrastim and the long-acting G-CSFs

prevention of febrile neutropenia

Filgrastim stimulates neutrophil production to shorten the duration of neutropenia — daily injections. Pegfilgrastim and eflapegrastim use pegylation to block renal clearance (once per chemotherapy cycle); efbemalenograstim alfa uses an IgG2 Fc fusion instead, avoiding PEG allergy. Signature side effect: bone pain — expected, not harmful. Do not give within ~24 hours of cytotoxic chemotherapy.

⚠️ Complement inhibitors and meningococcal disease

In paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria — a deficiency of the complement regulators CD55 and CD59 causing intravascular hemolysis, and a highly prothrombotic state where thrombosis, not anemia, is what kills patients — the drugs are complement inhibitors: eculizumab and ravulizumab (C5), pegcetacoplan (C3), and iptacopan, the first oral agent, which inhibits complement factor B.

Blocking terminal complement removes the exact defence the body uses against encapsulated organisms. All complement inhibitors carry a boxed warning for serious, life-threatening meningococcal infection, and patients must be vaccinated against Neisseria meningitidis before starting. Note the parallel with asplenia in Section 10 — same organisms, different missing defence.

Memory hook: “C3 catches more than C5.” Blocking higher in the cascade stops more hemolysis — C5 blockers stop only the intravascular half, leaving C3b-coated cells to be eaten in the spleen; C3 and factor B blockers stop both.

🧠 Hemophilia A and B — four strategies, and the mechanism each one reveals

Hemophilia A is insufficient factor VIII (1 : 5,000 live births); hemophilia B is insufficient factor IX (1 : 25,000). Both are X-linked. The mechanism they share: factors IXa and VIIIa together activate factor X, and that is the step both diseases break.

  1. Replace it. Intravenous recombinant or plasma-derived factor concentrate. Simple and effective — but requires frequent venous access, and some patients develop inhibitors (antibodies against replacement factor) that make it stop working.
  2. Mimic it — emicizumab. A bispecific antibody: one arm binds factor IX, the other binds factor X, holding them together. That is all factor VIII ever did — it is a clamp, not an enzyme. Subcutaneous, and because it is not factor VIII, anti-factor-VIII inhibitors do not neutralize it.
  3. Insert the gene. Adeno-associated virus vectors delivering a functional factor gene to liver cells — fidanacogene elparvovec and etranacogene dezaparvovec (hemophilia B), valoctocogene roxaparvovec (hemophilia A).
  4. Rebalance — works in A and B. If you cannot raise the procoagulant side, lower the anticoagulant side. Anti-TFPI antibodies marstacimab (without inhibitors) and concizumab (with inhibitors) block tissue factor pathway inhibitor; the siRNA fitusiran degrades antithrombin mRNA. The predictable adverse event for all of them is thrombosis — you are deliberately removing a natural anticoagulant.

Memory hooks: emicizumab is a molecular clothespin (bispecific = two arms). And “with or without inhibitors” is the tie-breaker: Concizumab = Complicated patient (WITH inhibitors); marstacimab and fitusiran, without.

Scope note: von Willebrand disease, the acquired bleeding disorders and the full bleeding-disorder laboratory workup belong to a lecture we do not have. Study guide objectives 39, 48 and 82 are marked partial for that reason.

Q: A 34-year-old with celiac disease and iron deficiency anemia has failed three months of ferrous sulfate. Her ferritin is still 6 ng/mL. What went wrong, and what do you do?

Answer

Iron malabsorption — celiac disease damages the duodenum, which is the only site where iron is absorbed. No oral dose will work reliably. (Check adherence too, since gastrointestinal side effects are the commonest reason for apparent failure — but here the pathology explains it.)

Switch to intravenous iron, which bypasses the duodenum, the acid requirement and the hepcidin door entirely. Give it slowly with observation for infusion reactions; if she has asthma or multiple drug allergies, premedicate with methylprednisolone 125 mg IV — not diphenhydramine. If she is receiving repeat courses of ferric carboxymaltose, check a phosphate level.

Q: A patient with chronic kidney disease on epoetin alfa has a hemoglobin that has risen from 9.2 to 10.9 g/dL over two weeks. The nephrology fellow wants to increase the dose to reach 12. What do you say?

Answer

Both parts of that plan violate the boxed warnings.

The target is wrong. Targeting hemoglobin above 11 g/dL increases death, serious cardiovascular events and stroke in chronic kidney disease, with no additional benefit. The goal is the lowest dose needed to avoid transfusion, not a normal hemoglobin.

The rate is also wrong. The hemoglobin has risen 1.7 g/dL in 2 weeks. The rule is to decrease the dose if it rises more than 1 g/dL in any 2-week period, because an excessive rate causes or worsens hypertension — the most common adverse effect, occurring in up to a third of treated patients. Reduce the dose, check the blood pressure, and confirm iron stores are adequate.

Q: A patient is admitted with methotrexate toxicity. Someone has written for high-dose folic acid. Why will that not work, and what should be given?

Answer

Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) — and DHFR is exactly the enzyme required to convert folic acid into its biologically active form. Giving folic acid hands the cell a substrate it cannot activate.

Give folinic acid (leucovorin). It is already past the DHFR step and is converted directly to active folate forms, restoring the folate pool without needing the blocked enzyme. That is what “leucovorin rescue” means — you are not reversing methotrexate; you are handing the cell an activated folate it can still use.

Q: Why would you choose luspatercept rather than an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia?

Answer

Because thalassemia's problem is ineffective erythropoiesis, not an absent signal. The marrow has plenty of precursors — it is hypercellular — and they are dying before release because unpaired globin chains destroy them. An ESA amplifies the build order, which would only shout louder at an assembly line already jammed at the end.

Luspatercept is an erythroid maturation agent: it helps late-stage red cells complete development, unblocking the actual bottleneck. Different lever, matched to the mechanism.

Section 17 · Infection

Sepsis — Signs, Scores, Microbial Triggers and Management

The body's extreme response to an infection, resulting in life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response. Rather than dealing with the infection, the immune system attacks “self”.

Abbreviations used in this section SIRS Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome · SOFA Sequential Organ Failure Assessment · qSOFA quick SOFA · NEWS2 National Early Warning Score, version 2 · MEWS Modified Early Warning Score · AVPU Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive · MODS Multi-Organ Dysfunction Syndrome · PAMPs Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns · DAMPs Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns · LPS lipopolysaccharide · IL-1 / IL-6 interleukin-1 / interleukin-6 · CRP C-reactive protein · aPTT activated partial thromboplastin time · PaO₂ / FiO₂ arterial oxygen partial pressure / fraction of inspired oxygen · CMS the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services · PSS post-sepsis syndrome
🔑 The one sentence that organizes everything

Because the damage comes from the host response rather than the pathogen directly: no single organism defines sepsis, cultures are negative in 30–50% of cases, and — as the outline states twice — no assessment or diagnostic criterion has sufficient sensitivity or specificity. That is why there are five competing scoring systems rather than one test.

The three terms, in order of severity

  1. Early sepsis. Infection and bacteremia are risk factors — the setup, not the diagnosis itself.
  2. Sepsis. Life-threatening, time-dependent organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. The phrase time-dependent is what justifies the treatment bundle.
  3. Septic shock. A subset of sepsis in which underlying circulatory AND cellular/metabolic abnormalities are profound enough to substantially increase mortality. Can lead to multi-organ dysfunction (MODS, an older term).
🧠 How to keep them straight

Infection/bacteremia → risk factor. Add organ dysfunction → sepsis. Add profound circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormality → septic shock. Each step is a strict subset of the one before, and each adds one requirement. Note that septic shock is not simply hypotension — the cellular/metabolic derangement is part of the definition, which is why lactate sits in the treatment bundle.

Five scores, none sufficient ★ HY

ScoreWhat it isStatus / useParameters
SIRSSystemic Inflammatory Response SyndromeNo longer a defining criterion for sepsis — but still popular, and used by the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid ServicesMeasurable responses to stress (below)
SOFASequential Organ Failure AssessmentMore specific; better predictive validity than SIRSNeurologic, liver, kidney, blood/hemodynamics
qSOFAquick SOFABedside assessment outside the emergency room3 criteria
NEWS2National Early Warning ScoreAssesses risk of death from sepsisAggregate of 6 parameters
MEWSModified Early Warning ScoreMore sensitive5 parameters
🌡️

SIRS criteria — and note the bidirectionality

  • Temperature: hypothermia (< 38 °C) or hyperthermia (> 38 °C)
  • Heart rate: tachycardia > 90 bpm
  • Respiratory: respiratory rate > 20/min, OR PaCO₂ < 32 mmHg
  • White cell count: leukopenia < 4,000/µL, OR leukocytosis > 12,000/µL, OR > 10% bands

Three of the four can be tripped in either direction. A septic patient can be hypothermic and leukopenic, which is easy to misread as “not infected”. That bidirectionality is a favourite exam trap.

⚡

qSOFA — three bedside criteria

  • Respiratory rate ≥ 22/min — the most sensitive early vital sign change
  • Systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mmHg — note ≤ 100, not < 90; qSOFA catches patients before frank hypotension
  • Altered mentation, assessed by Glasgow Coma Scale

SOFA: assesses neurologic, liver, kidney and blood/hemodynamic systems. A score ≥ 2 indicates a mortality risk of approximately 10%.

🔑 Distinguishing NEWS2 from MEWS

Both are early-warning scores built from vital signs. NEWS2 has 6 parameters (respiration rate, oxygen saturation, systolic blood pressure, pulse, consciousness level, temperature). MEWS has 5 (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, AVPU/mental status) and is the more sensitive of the two. Every MEWS parameter also appears in NEWS2 — oxygen saturation is the one NEWS2 adds.

Risk factors and epidemiology

⚠️

Risk factors

  • Intensive care unit admission
  • Bacteremia
  • Age ≥ 65, and children < 1 year (risk increased if premature)
  • Pregnancy
  • Immune suppression comorbidities — diabetes, chemotherapy, recent organ transplant
  • Community-acquired pneumonia
  • Prior hospitalization
  • Genetic factors reducing immune response or pathogen recognition
📊

United States figures

  • 1.7 million cases per year
  • ~350,000 deaths per year
  • $62 billion annual cost
  • High re-hospitalization rate

Source of infection, in order: respiratory > urinary > abdominal > head > other (skin, gastrointestinal, meningitis). Respiratory first is the single most useful fact here — and it explains why community-acquired pneumonia appears in the risk factor list.

Etiologies — bacterial first, but nothing excluded

  • Bacterial etiology is more common than the others. No organism is detected in 30–50% of cases.
  • Gram-positives are the most commonly identified: S. aureus, Enterococcus, S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes.
  • Gram-negatives remain important: E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter.
  • 20% of cases are polymicrobial. Viral causes are often underdiagnosed. Fungal (Candida) cases are increasing in the immunocompromised.
Initial infection siteOrganisms
RespiratoryS. pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae b, E. coli and other aerobic gram-negative bacilli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae (alcohol use), Legionella pneumophila
Urinary tractE. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Enterococcus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Proteus
AbdominalE. coli, Bacteroides fragilis, Candida, mixed anaerobes
Skin / soft tissueS. pyogenes, S. aureus, aerobic gram-negative bacilli, Clostridium and other anaerobes, Pseudomonas aeruginosa
MeningitisS. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes
ClassAgentsContext
ViralInfluenza, RSV, Covid, adenovirus, rhinovirusCommon respiratory agents
Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirusImmunocompromised patients
Herpes simplex 1, enterovirusNeonates to young children
Dengue, yellow fever, EbolaTropical / subtropical areas
FungalCandida (albicans, auris) — 80%; Aspergillus — 10%Associated with risk factors
ParasiticPlasmodium, Schistosoma, Leishmania, EchinococcusEndemic niches

Microbial triggers — PAMPs and DAMPs ★ HY

🦠

PAMPs

Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns — molecular signatures carried by the organism itself.

💥

DAMPs

Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns — released from the host's own damaged tissues. This is the mechanism by which viral infection triggers sepsis.

ClassTrigger typeSpecific molecules
Bacterial — gram-positivePAMPsLipoteichoic acid, cell wall peptidoglycan
Bacterial — gram-negativePAMPsLipopolysaccharide (LPS) — the most prominent trigger overall
Bacterial — otherPAMPsSuper-antigens (TSST 1&2, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin), also DNA, RNA, surface glycoproteins
ViralDAMPsReleased from virus-damaged tissue → cascade of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6)
FungalPAMPsβ-glucans, mannans, chitin — all polysaccharides
ParasiticBothPAMPs and DAMPs
🪝 The cleanest pairings to memorize

Gram-negative → LPS. Gram-positive → lipoteichoic acid + peptidoglycan. Fungal → β-glucans, mannans, chitin (one rule covers all three: polysaccharides). Viral → DAMPs, not PAMPs — the exception in the list, and therefore the likely question.

The sepsis paradigm — mechanism

  1. The patient is injured by some means — the initiating insult.
  2. Host defences activate — release of inflammatory cytokines, plus activation of other agents that exert control over bodily systems.
  3. Persistent inflammation → the cascade to organ failure. Endothelial dysfunction and ischemic tissue injury → sequential organ damage/failure → activation of cell death pathways: necrosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, autophagy.
🧠 Why “sequential” matters

Organ failure in sepsis is sequential, not simultaneous — which is precisely what the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment is built to track. The mechanism and the scoring system share the same word for the same reason.

Laboratory findings ★ HY

Laboratory featureFinding / thresholdWhat it reflects
White blood cell countLeukocytosis > 12,000/µL, leukopenia < 4,000/µL, or a normal count with > 10% immature formsBidirectional — a normal count with a left shift still qualifies
Platelet countThrombocytopenia < 100,000/µLConsumption / coagulopathy
Coagulation> 1.5 mg/dL, or aPTT > 60 secondsCoagulopathy
CreatinineIncreased > 0.5 mg/dLRenal organ dysfunction
Lactic acidElevatedTissue hypoperfusion — and it is in the treatment bundle
BilirubinTotal > 4 mg/dLHepatic dysfunction; clinical jaundice
C-reactive proteinElevatedNon-specific inflammation
ProcalcitoninElevatedIndicative of a BACTERIAL etiology — the one cause-specific marker on the list
Arterial oxygenHypoxemia — PaO₂/FiO₂ < 300Pulmonary organ dysfunction
Plasma glucoseHyperglycemia > 140 mg/dLStress metabolic response
Urine outputOliguria < 0.5 mL/kg/hrRenal hypoperfusion
CortisolBaseline < 10 mg/dLAdrenal insufficiency
Bacterial culturesNegative in 30–50% of casesA negative culture does not exclude sepsis
Acid–baseMetabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosisThe classic simultaneous pairing — lactate from hypoperfusion, plus tachypnea

Other clinical findings: SIRS-like symptoms, peripheral vasodilation and shock, altered mental acuity, jaundice, thrombocytopenia.

Treatment and prognosis

  1. Bactericidal antimicrobial treatment. Note the outline specifies bactericidal, not merely bacteriostatic.
  2. Intravenous fluids. Addresses the peripheral vasodilation and hypoperfusion.
  3. Lactate measurement. The marker of the cellular/metabolic abnormality in the septic shock definition.
  4. Assess tissue perfusion. Confirms whether the fluids are working.
  5. Vasopressors, when fluids alone cannot maintain perfusion pressure.

Plus: surgical removal or drainage of the infection site — source control; and oxygen therapy.

🔑 Why the bundle is a bundle

Sepsis is time-dependent organ dysfunction. That single word justifies delivering all five elements together and early, rather than sequentially as results return.

OutcomeFigure
Mortality (patients with risk factors)10–52%
Post-sepsis syndrome50% of sepsis survivors
Survival in young / healthy patients90%

Q: A septic patient has a normal white blood cell count. Does this argue against the diagnosis?

Answer

No. The laboratory criterion is satisfied by leukocytosis (> 12,000/µL), leukopenia (< 4,000/µL), or a normal white count with > 10% immature forms — a left shift with a normal total. The same bidirectional logic runs through SIRS, where both hypothermia and hyperthermia qualify. In sepsis, a “normal-looking” number can still be an abnormal response.

Q: Which sepsis assessment is described as more specific with better predictive validity than SIRS, and what does a score of ≥ 2 indicate?

Answer

SOFA — the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment. A score ≥ 2 indicates a mortality risk of approximately 10%. It assesses neurologic, liver, kidney and blood/hemodynamic systems. Remember that SIRS is no longer a defining criterion for sepsis, though it remains in use by the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

Q: Name the four cell death pathways activated by persistent inflammation in sepsis, and the two upstream events that precede them.

Answer

Cell death pathways: necrosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, autophagy.

The two upstream events are endothelial dysfunction and ischemic tissue injury, which together produce sequential organ damage and failure. The chain to reproduce: persistent inflammation → endothelial dysfunction + ischemic tissue injury → sequential organ failure → cell death pathways.

Q: A patient develops sepsis from an intra-abdominal source. Which anaerobe should be at the front of your differential, and what proportion of sepsis cases overall are polymicrobial?

Answer

Bacteroides fragilis — the abdominal site is the one explicitly paired with B. fragilis and mixed anaerobes, alongside E. coli and Candida. 20% of sepsis cases are polymicrobial, and abdominal sources are a major reason why.

Section 18 · Infection

HIV — Structural Genes, the Replication Cycle, and the Antiretroviral Drug Map

Every antiretroviral drug class is named for the step it blocks. Learn the cycle as a table and the pharmacology becomes recall rather than memorization.

Abbreviations used in this section ART antiretroviral therapy · RNA / DNA ribonucleic acid / deoxyribonucleic acid · RT reverse transcriptase · IN integrase · PI protease inhibitor · NRTI nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor · NNRTI non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor · INSTI integrase strand transfer inhibitor · PIC pre-integration complex · RTC reverse transcription complex · gp120 / gp41 glycoprotein 120 / 41 · CCR5 / CXCR4 chemokine co-receptors · PrEP / PEP pre- / post-exposure prophylaxis · aa amino acid
🔑 The central sequence

HIV infects CD4 T cells → viral RNA is reverse transcribed into double-stranded DNA → that DNA integrates into the host chromosome (the provirus) → the infection becomes persistent and latent → the immune system is progressively damaged → opportunistic infections and malignancies follow.

Why “retrovirus”: it uses reverse transcriptase to form a double-stranded DNA intermediate, reversing the usual DNA → RNA direction. Baltimore Group VI.

1

Genetic diversity

Highly mutable. Reverse transcriptase has a high error rate, which is the direct source of drug-resistance mutations.

2

Latency

Integrated provirus can sit transcriptionally silent, invisible to drugs that only target actively replicating virus.

3

It attacks the immune response itself

Targets CD4 T cells and macrophages — the very cells that would clear it.

Structure and the three structural genes ★ HY

The virion is 100–150 nm, with an outer envelope bearing two glycoprotein spikes (gp120, gp41) and containing two copies of single-stranded RNA. The major structural genes are pol, gag and env.

GeneProductFunctionExam hook
pol (polymerase)Reverse transcriptaseRNA-dependent DNA polymerase — synthesizes the HIV provirusHigh error rate → the source of HIV diversity and of resistance
IntegraseIntegrates provirus DNA into the host genomeThe irreversible step; target of the INSTI class
Protease (aspartyl)Cleaves the precursor proteins of the pol and gag genesWithout it, virions are immature and non-infectious
gag (group-specific antigen) — a p55 precursor cleaved by VIRAL proteasep24Capsid core antigen; also brings the pre-integration complex into the host chromosomeEASIEST TO DETECT IN SERA — this is the p24 antigen used in 4th-generation testing
p17Matrix protein, lining the inner envelope—
p6 / p7 / p9Nucleocapsid proteins; bind the viral RNA genome—
env (envelope) — a 160 kDa precursor cleaved by HOST proteasegp120The binding protein — binds the CD4 receptor plus a chemokine co-receptor, CCR5 or CXCR4Target of fostemsavir and maraviroc
gp41The fusion protein — contains the “fusogenic domain” enabling fusion with the host membraneTarget of enfuvirtide
🪝 Memory hook — who cleaves what

gag and pol precursors are cleaved by VIRAL protease — which is exactly why protease inhibitors work. The env precursor is cleaved by HOST protease — which is why they do not touch it.

Regulatory / accessory geneFunction
tat *Activator of transcription — also inhibits T-cell proliferation
revRegulates viral expression — enhances expression
vifVirion infectivity
vpr *Nuclear incorporation of the pre-integration complex; enhances replication; arrests host cell cycle progression
vpuEnhances viral release; downregulates CD4 surface expression
nef *Negative regulatory function — protects HIV-infected cells from killing by T lymphocytes

* Starred genes are of increased interest for antiretroviral development.

The replication cycle → drug class → resistance ★ HY

StepWhat happensDrug class & exampleResistance mechanism
1. Attachment / fusiongp120 binds CD4 plus CCR5 or CXCR4 → conformational change exposes gp41, which fuses with the membrane → cell entryFostemsavir — attachment inhibitor, binds gp120A high rate of gp120 amino acid substitutions reduces binding efficiency
Maraviroc — CCR5 antagonistgp120 substitution that facilitates binding to the drug-altered receptor conformation
Enfuvirtide — fusion inhibitor, binds gp41Amino acid substitution in gp41 → no drug binding
Ibalizumab — post-attachment entry inhibitor, a monoclonal antibodyBlocks CD4 receptors — virus can attach but cannot enter
2. UncoatingViral genome released; capsid material chaperones the pre-integration complex into the nucleus — which is why the capsid is itself a drug target——
3. Reverse transcriptionSynthesis of complementary double-stranded DNA (the provirus). The reverse transcription complex transitions into the pre-integration complex and is transported to the nucleusNRTIs — competitive binding to RT → chain termination. Zidovudine (thymidine analogue), tenofovir (adenosine analogue). Often used in pairsRT point mutations reduce affinity of NRTI binding — generally requires accumulated mutations
NNRTIs — non-competitive, allosteric; cause conformational change in RT. Efavirenz, doravirineA SINGLE point mutation on a conserved RT domain can inactivate ALL class members — a much lower genetic barrier
Lenacapavir — capsid inhibitor; obstructs PIC transport to the nucleusOne capsid mutation confers > 80,000-fold resistance
4. IntegrationIntegration into the host genome via integrase — the irreversible step that creates the latent reservoirINSTIs — prevent strand transfer of viral DNA into the host genome. Raltegravir; cabotegravir, also available long-acting injectableMutations altering integrase structure → decreased drug binding
5. Assembly, budding, maturation, releaseAssembly near the cell surface, budding, then protease cleaves the gag and gag/pol precursors into p6, p7, p17, p24, RT and INProtease inhibitors — atazanavir, darunavir. Prevent maturation; virions remain immature and non-infectiousResistance is UNCOMMON unless the patient was previously treated with a protease inhibitor — a notably high genetic barrier
Lenacapavir again — disrupts assembly of progeny capsidAs above
AdjunctNot a step in the cycleCobicistat (and ritonavir) — pharmacokinetic enhancers. They inhibit metabolic breakdown (CYP3A4), raising antiretroviral levelsNOT antiretrovirals themselves — a classic distractor
🩺 The resistance contrast worth memorizing ★ HY

Three points on a spectrum of genetic barrier:

  • NNRTIs — the lowest barrier. One point mutation knocks out the entire class, because all members bind the same allosteric pocket.
  • Protease inhibitors — a high barrier. Resistance is uncommon unless previously PI-treated.
  • Lenacapavir — the extreme case in the other direction: a single capsid mutation confers a > 80,000-fold shift.

The upstream cause is always the same: reverse transcriptase's high error rate generates the variant pool that selection then acts on.

Prophylaxis — PrEP and PEP

ProductAgent(s)Route
TruvadaEmtricitabine / tenofovir disoproxil fumarateOral
DescovyEmtricitabine / tenofovir alafenamideOral
ApretudeCabotegravirIntramuscular injection
YeztugoLenacapavirInjection and oral

Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is given after occupational exposure to blood or body fluids — the example regimen is tenofovir + emtricitabine with raltegravir.

Transmission — and the two facts tested as negatives

  • Modes: sexual; contaminated body fluids; vertical (mother to infant); occupational; shared needles.
  • Spread primarily in blood, semen and cervical secretions.
  • Primary target: helper T cells and monocytes.
  • The agent is easily inactivated outside the host.
  • No insect vectors have been identified.
⚠️ Why those last two are examined

They rule out fomite and vector transmission, which distinguishes HIV from many other infectious agents on a differential. Both are frequently tested as negatives.

Opportunistic infections and malignancies — three tiers ★ HY

  • Most common organisms: Toxoplasma gondii, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Candida, Cryptococcus neoformans, M. tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium complex, herpes simplex 1 and 2, varicella-zoster, cytomegalovirus.
  • Less common, in specific exposure or geographic contexts: Leishmania, Trypanosoma cruzi, Bartonella, Listeria monocytogenes, Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides, Cryptosporidium.
  • Neoplastic / preneoplastic: Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas, HPV-associated lesions, and the demyelinating disease progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
VirusAssociated disease

⚠️ Scope note on Bartonella

Bartonella henselae appears here only as an HIV opportunist causing bacillary angiomatosis. The full study guide objective — the etiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis and treatment of cat scratch disease and bacillary angiomatosis — needs its own lecture, so objective 30 is marked partial in the coverage map.

Q: Which HIV protein is easiest to detect in serum, which gene encodes it, and why does that matter for testing?

Answer

p24, the capsid protein, encoded by the gag gene — cleaved from the p55 precursor by viral protease.

It matters because p24 antigen becomes detectable before antibodies do. Pairing p24 antigen detection with antibody detection in a combination immunoassay is exactly what lets 4th-generation testing catch acute infection, weeks before an antibody-only test would turn positive.

Q: A patient's virus develops a single point mutation in a conserved domain of reverse transcriptase. Which drug class is most likely to be rendered entirely ineffective, and why does the other reverse-transcriptase class fare better?

Answer

The NNRTIs (efavirenz, doravirine). A single point mutation on a conserved RT domain can inactivate all members of the class, because they all bind the same allosteric pocket non-competitively.

NRTIs fare better because their resistance mechanism is different: point mutations reduce the affinity of NRTI binding rather than abolishing it, and NRTIs bind competitively at the active site as nucleoside analogues — so they generally require accumulated mutations rather than one.

Q: Match each agent to its replication step: fostemsavir, raltegravir, darunavir, enfuvirtide, doravirine, lenacapavir, cobicistat.

Answer
  • Fostemsavir — Step 1, attachment (binds gp120)
  • Enfuvirtide — Step 1, fusion (binds gp41)
  • Doravirine — Step 3, reverse transcription (NNRTI, allosteric)
  • Lenacapavir — Steps 2/3 and 5, capsid (blocks PIC transport; disrupts progeny capsid assembly)
  • Raltegravir — Step 4, integration (INSTI)
  • Darunavir — Step 5, maturation (protease inhibitor)
  • Cobicistat — none of them. It is a pharmacokinetic enhancer, not an antiretroviral

Q: Name the viral agent behind each of these AIDS-associated conditions: Kaposi sarcoma, B-cell lymphoma, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and cervical or anal squamous cell carcinoma.

Answer
  • Kaposi sarcoma → HHV-8
  • B-cell lymphoma (Hodgkin / non-Hodgkin) → Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4)
  • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy → JC virus, a polyomavirus
  • Cervical / anal / oral squamous cell carcinoma → HPV types 16 and 18

All four are oncogenic viruses that an intact immune system would normally hold in check — which is why they define the neoplastic tier of opportunistic disease.

HIV — Diagnosis, Staging, Opportunistic Infection versus IRIS, and Management

Three cases span the arc of the disease: acute retroviral syndrome, a newly diagnosed outpatient, and advanced AIDS with an opportunistic infection.

Abbreviations used in this section Ag/Ab antigen/antibody · p24 Ag the HIV-1 viral core protein antigen · NAT nucleic acid test (the HIV-1 RNA test, also written RNA PCR) · ARS acute retroviral syndrome (= primary HIV infection) · CDC Centers for Disease Control and Prevention · OI opportunistic infection · IRIS immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome · PJP Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (older name PCP) · TMP/SMX trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole · LDH lactate dehydrogenase · A–a gradient the alveolar-to-arterial oxygen difference · TDF / TAF tenofovir disoproxil fumarate / tenofovir alafenamide · U = U undetectable equals untransmittable

Acute retroviral syndrome — the diagnosis that gets missed

🔑 Why it matters
  • After acquisition, more than 50% develop a transient symptomatic illness — which then resolves on its own.
  • Features are nonspecific and it is most often confused with mononucleosis.
  • Transmission risk is at its highest here — very high HIV RNA plus the person does not know their status.
  • Keep it on the differential for any teenager or 20-something with non-exudative pharyngitis + rash + splenomegaly + atypical lymphocytosis.

The key discriminator from Group A streptococcal pharyngitis: acute retroviral syndrome gives NON-exudative pharyngitis. Frequencies from the lecture: fever ~75–80%, fatigue ~68–78%, myalgia ~48%, rash ~48–51%, headache ~45–54%, pharyngitis ~40%.

🩺 Two clinical pearls that predate modern testing
  • Hypergammaglobulinemia with a reversed albumin:globulin ratio was the historical tip-off for HIV when serology took 6 weeks to 3 months — especially alongside atypical lymphocytosis. It is still a useful clue.
  • New-onset or unusually aggressive seborrheic dermatitis — classically at the glabella (between the eyebrows) and nasolabial folds — should make you think about HIV and screen for it.

The three periods — why the window exists ★ HY

PeriodApproximate timingWhat is detectable
Eclipse periodDay 0 – ~10 daysNothing. No diagnostic test can detect HIV in this interval
Acute infection~10 – 50 daysHIV RNA rises first, then p24 antigen appears and peaks (~day 30), then antibodies begin
Established (chronic) infection> ~50 days onwardHIV antibodies rise and persist; RNA settles at the viral set point; p24 falls away

Seroconversion is the interval between acquiring HIV and the first detection of anti-HIV antibodies — the window period. How long it is depends on the sensitivity of the assay, which is why modern practice uses 4th- or 5th-generation assays that also detect p24 antigen, catching infection weeks before antibodies appear.

The CDC testing algorithm — three tiers ★ HY

  1. HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay, with HIV-1 p24 antigen. Non-reactive → stop. But if acute infection is clinically suspected, go straight to an HIV-1 NAT, because of the eclipse period.
  2. HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay — performed as a reflex when step 1 is reactive. Resolves to HIV-1 positive, HIV-2 positive, untypeable, or indeterminate/negative. If antibodies are detected → manage as HIV infection.
  3. HIV-1 nucleic acid test (NAT / RNA PCR) — reflexed when the differentiation assay is negative or indeterminate. RNA detected here = acute HIV-1 infection; antibodies have not yet developed. RNA not detected → negative; offer prevention services including PrEP and PEP.
⚠️ “Why not just do the NAT first?”

The nucleic acid test does detect HIV earlier. But it is roughly 3× the cost, far more complex for laboratories to run, and carries a real false-positive potential — particularly in low-risk individuals. That is why it sits at tier 3, not tier 1.

Note also: the Western blot is obsolete. It detects antibodies only, has a longer detection window, inferior sensitivity, and cannot differentiate HIV-1 from HIV-2. It was the standard until 2014.

🩺 False positives are rare

The false-positive rate for HIV testing with reflex is 0.22%. Practically: when a modern 4th/5th-generation assay with reflex is positive, the patient has HIV. Patients will sometimes not believe the result — these tests are very good.

CD4 count versus viral load — the single most testable distinction ★ HY

🛡️

CD4 T-cell count

Degree of immune system impairment. Determines the risk of opportunistic infections and who needs prophylaxis. It is the staging variable.

🦠

HIV RNA viral load

Active viral replication. Determines drug selection and monitors treatment response. It is the transmission variable — the basis of U = U.

🔑 Two thresholds that are NOT the same number
  • CD4 < 200 cells/µL (or < 14%) defines AIDS — CDC stage 3. So does the presence of an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection, at any CD4 count.
  • CD4 < 50 cells/µL is where opportunistic infection risk is greatest.

Careful: community-acquired pneumonia by itself, without evidence of a compromised immune system, is not an opportunistic infection. In a patient with an impaired immune system, the same pneumonia does count — and two or more episodes of bacterial pneumonia within 12 months is itself AIDS-defining.

StageTimingCD4 countCD4 %Opportunistic infections
Acute (stage 1)2–4 weeks post-infection≥ 500/µL≥ 29%None
Chronic (clinical latency)Many years (~10)FallingFallingNone — few symptoms
AIDS (stage 3)~3 years' survival untreated< 200/µL< 14%Onset of opportunistic infections
🩺 The lymphocyte shortcut

An absolute lymphocyte count < 1,000 cells/mm³ predicts a CD4 count < 200 cells/mm³. Useful because the complete blood count often returns before HIV-specific testing — it tells you immediately whether to start thinking about prophylaxis.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia ★ HY

🧠 Why it is an “atypical” fungus — and why that dictates the drug
  • Classified as a fungus on RNA, cell wall and key enzymes — but it does not grow in fungal culture.
  • Its cell wall contains cholesterol, not ergosterol — which is precisely why the standard antifungals that target ergosterol synthesis do not work, and why the treatment is TMP/SMX.
  • The cell wall is rich in β-1,3-D-glucan — the basis of the serum β-D-glucan test.
  • Main risk factor is immunosuppression of any cause, not just HIV: kidney transplant, chemotherapy, chronic steroids.
  • Airborne transmission; exists in a latent state within alveolar macrophages.
DomainFindings
The symptom triadFever (80–100%), non-productive cough (95%), progressive dyspnea (95%). 5–10% asymptomatic
Physical examinationFever > 38.1 °C in > 80%; tachypnea 60%; crackles and rhonchi — but a normal chest exam in ~50%; frequent co-infection with thrush
CD4 thresholdTypically < 200 cells/µL
Gas exchangePoor oxygenation with an increased A–a gradient
BiomarkersElevated LDH; elevated 1,3-β-D-glucan (> 80 pg/mL)
ImagingDiffuse interstitial or alveolar infiltrates, may be upper-lobe predominant; ground-glass opacities with peripheral sparing on CT; risk of pneumothorax. The chest radiograph can be normal in up to 25% — but a normal high-resolution CT argues strongly against PJP
🩺 PJP management
  • Treat empirically when suspicion is high — CD4 < 200, hypoxemia with an increased A–a gradient, classic radiographic features. Do not wait for confirmation.
  • TMP/SMX is the preferred regimen — oral for mild–moderate, intravenous for severe. Dose by weight on the trimethoprim component.
  • Add corticosteroids in moderate–severe disease — they reduce respiratory failure and mortality. Indications: worsening respiratory symptoms with PaO₂ < 70 mmHg or an A–a gradient ≥ 35 mmHg. Prednisone for 21 days.
  • Expect worsening for the first 2–3 days after starting treatment — killing the organism releases inflammatory material. This early worsening is NOT IRIS; it is too soon.
  • Start ART within 2 weeks of beginning PJP treatment, to restore immune function.
  • Prophylaxis: TMP/SMX if CD4 < 200 and not on ART, continued until the immune system reconstitutes.

Opportunistic infection versus IRIS ★ HY

🧠 Definition

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome is an exaggerated immune response to a variety of pathogens, occurring in response to ART-mediated recovery of the immune system. The immune system comes back online and overreacts to things that were sitting latent.

📉

Paradoxical IRIS

The opportunistic infection is already known. You are treating it, you start ART, and symptoms worsen. Example: a PJP patient improves past the expected 2–3 day dip, then at 1–2 weeks develops worsening hypoxemia and infiltrates and requires intubation.

🎭

Unmasking (ART-associated) IRIS

The opportunistic infection was undiagnosed until ART was started. No known OI; you start ART; the recovering immune system produces inflammation that reveals the infection.

Clinical featureOpportunistic infectionIRIS
Risk factorsLow CD4; advanced HIV/AIDSAdvanced disease with low pre-treatment CD4; a robust virologic and immunologic response; temporal association between ART start and symptom onset
CD4 countLow — often < 100/µLOften improving (though pre-treatment CD4 was low and viral load high)
When it occursLate in the course, as CD4 fallsIn the first few months after starting ART — median 48 days
Associated diseasesPredominantly infectious — Cryptococcus, TB/MAC, PJP, JC virus, CMVImmune-mediated as well — sarcoidosis, autoimmune thyroid disease, Kaposi sarcoma, plus infectious causes
Relationship to ARTOccurs prior to ART initiationOccurs while or after ART initiation — in 10–20% of patients
Regimen dependence—The specific ART regimen chosen does not affect IRIS risk
⚠️ The answer is not to delay ART

Delaying costs more than it saves. The correct approach is to anticipate IRIS, counsel the patient that worsening may occur, and keep it on your differential when the patient deteriorates on day 10 instead of improving.

The management plan

  1. The conversation is the intervention, not the preamble. Shared decision-making and motivational interviewing. Identify structural barriers — housing, transport, cost, prior authorization, stigma. Adherence is the whole disease.
  2. Start ART as soon as possible — ideally within 7 days, and “same day” is acceptable and increasingly preferred. Exclude pregnancy in anyone of childbearing potential, and screen for sexually transmitted infections.
  3. Define the goal: U = U. Plasma HIV RNA below the level of detection — the CDC threshold is < 200 copies/mL. Undetectable = Untransmittable. Check viral load every 3–4 months; small temporary rises (“blips”) are not immediately alarming — follow the trend.
  4. Prophylax by CD4 count. See the table below.
  5. Immunize — and know the live vaccine rule.
  6. Prevent onward transmission — PrEP and PEP for partners and contacts.
🔑 The evidence behind U = U — the PARTNER trial

Observed male–female and male–male couples (~3,000 individuals) across more than 74,000 condomless sex episodes. Zero HIV transmissions to HIV-negative partners while the partner with HIV maintained a durable undetectable viral load for ≥ 6 months.

CD4 thresholdProphylaxisTarget infection
< 200 cells/µLTMP/SMX (if not on ART; continue until immune reconstitution)Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
< 200 cells/µLCheck cryptococcal antigenCryptococcus (meningitis)
< 100 cells/µLProphylaxis in Toxoplasma IgG-positive patients — TMP/SMX covers bothToxoplasmosis encephalitis
AnyTreat latent tuberculosis if PPD or interferon-gamma release assay is positiveTuberculosis
⚠️ The live vaccine rule ★ HY

The three live vaccines — varicella, yellow fever, and MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) — may be given only when the CD4 count is ≥ 200 cells/µL. Two reasons: risk of vaccine-strain disease, and below that threshold the patient cannot mount an immunologic response, so you are wasting the dose.

Zoster: the old live attenuated vaccine is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients and in HIV with CD4 < 200. The recombinant vaccine (2 doses) is the one to use in immunocompromised patients, including all transplant recipients.

Give regardless of CD4 count: mpox, Tdap, COVID-19, influenza, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and recombinant zoster.

⚠️ The drug interaction you will be tested on ★ HY

Boosters — ritonavir and cobicistat — are added to raise antiretroviral levels by inhibiting cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4).

Combine a booster with an over-the-counter nasal corticosteroid and the steroid accumulates → iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and adrenal suppression. Nasal steroids are sold over the counter, so if you do not warn the patient, no one will. The same CYP3A4 pathway governs several statins. Always ask about over-the-counter drugs, supplements and herbal preparations at every visit — patients do not volunteer them.

QuestionPrEP — pre-exposure prophylaxisPEP — post-exposure prophylaxis
When is it taken?Before exposureAfter exposure — started within 72 hours, taken for a month
Who is it for?People without HIV at risk from sex or injection drug usePeople without HIV who may have been exposed — sex, sexual assault, occupational needlestick, shared injection equipment
How effective?Reduces sexual transmission by ~99%, injection-drug transmission by ~74%Reduces risk to roughly < 1% when taken correctly — but not always effective. Start as soon as possible
🩺 Three pearls before starting PrEP, and one worked example
  • Always exclude pregnancy and consider a sexually transmitted infection screen.
  • Check renal function and lipids. Both tenofovir formulations are toxic to the proximal tubule — worsening kidney function and Fanconi syndrome. TAF is the less nephrotoxic of the two, which is why it was developed. Both can drive lipids up substantially.
  • Screen for hepatitis B. Emtricitabine and tenofovir both treat active hepatitis B — so if a patient with active hepatitis B stops them, hepatitis B can rebound.

Needlestick on a surgical rotation: notify the surgeon immediately, notify human resources and health services, get tested, and consider starting PEP while results are pending. Do not wait for the source patient's results — the 72-hour window is what matters.

HIV as a disease of aging — chronic complications

🧠 “Inflammaging”

People with HIV now live close to normal lifespans, so the management plan has to extend past viral suppression into decades of cardiometabolic, bone, cognitive and cancer risk. Age-associated inflammation — “inflammaging” — is the major risk factor tying all the comorbidities together. It impacts both innate and adaptive immunity, increases cardiovascular disease, contributes to neurocognitive impairment, and accelerates functional limitation and frailty.

ComplicationFrequencyWhat to monitor / know
Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular diseaseUp to 40%People with HIV present with coronary artery disease roughly 10 years earlier. Standard risk tools underestimate risk — adjust upward by 1.5–2×; many target LDL < 70 mg/dL. Protease inhibitors raise cholesterol and triglycerides; INSTIs raise cholesterol more than triglycerides. Statin choice is an interaction problem (CYP3A4) — favour atorvastatin, low-dose rosuvastatin, or pitavastatin
Fat redistribution / lipodystrophy~50%Facial lipoatrophy; dorsocervical lipomatosis; abdominal lipohypertrophy. A marker of increased cardiovascular risk — epicardial and perivascular fat drives atherosclerosis directly
Diabetes and insulin resistanceNew-onset in ~14%Protease inhibitors downregulate the GLUT-4 transporter and reduce beta-cell insulin secretion; NRTIs contribute via mitochondrial toxicity. Hepatitis C co-infection raises incidence further
Bone lossMultifactorialIncreased osteoclastogenesis plus impaired osteoblasts. TDF causes proximal tubule dysfunction (Fanconi) → hypophosphatemia, accelerating bone loss — which is why baseline DEXA is recommended with TDF. Compounded by vitamin D deficiency and hypogonadism
Neurocognitive dysfunctionUp to ~50%HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder: asymptomatic → mild cognitive disorder → HIV-associated dementia. Affects attention, working memory, processing speed and executive function
⚠️ Scope note on age-related change

Study guide objective 79 asks about age-related changes generally and what should be monitored. What is here is the HIV-specific version — inflammaging and its comorbidities. The general hematologic changes of aging need another lecture, so that objective is marked partial.

Q: A 32-year-old presents after notification of a positive HIV 4th-generation antigen/antibody test. What is the next test?

A. HIV-1 Western blot · B. HIV-1 RNA PCR (NAT) · C. p24 antigen via ELISA · D. Genotype resistance testing · E. HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay

Answer — E

E. The HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay — it tells you which form of HIV you are dealing with, or whether the strain is untypeable.

A — no: the Western blot detects antibodies only, has a longer detection window, inferior sensitivity, and cannot differentiate HIV-1 from HIV-2. It was the standard until 2014. B — no: that is the third-tier confirmatory test. C — no: p24 is already included in the combination assay. D — no: genotype guides ART selection; it is not part of the diagnostic algorithm.

Q: Which lab value best predicts risk of opportunistic infections in HIV?

A. HIV RNA viral load · B. CD4 T-cell count · C. p24 antigen · D. HIV genotype · E. Absolute lymphocyte count

Answer — B

B. The CD4 T-cell count — the best measure of the degree of immune system impairment, and therefore of opportunistic infection risk and the need for prophylaxis.

A — viral load reflects active replication and drives drug selection; it is the transmission variable (U = U). C — p24 detects acute HIV-1 infection. D — genotype detects resistance mutations. E — useful as a surrogate (< 1,000/mm³ predicts CD4 < 200), but not the best predictor.

Q: A patient with AIDS (CD4 90 cells/µL) is being treated for PJP with TMP/SMX and prednisone. ART is started on day 10. On day 21 she develops worsening hypoxemia and new pulmonary infiltrates. Her HIV RNA has dropped from 1.5 million to 12,000 copies/mL and her CD4 has risen to 180. Most likely explanation?

Answer

Paradoxical IRIS. The tell-tale combination: a known, already-treated opportunistic infection, a short interval between OI treatment and ART start, and a robust virologic and immunologic response (falling viral load, rising CD4) occurring alongside clinical worsening.

The improving laboratory numbers are the clue that separate this from treatment failure or a second infection — in true OI progression the virology would not be improving. Timing also fits: IRIS occurs within the first few months of ART, median 48 days. Note that the expected 2–3 day post-treatment worsening of PJP happens far earlier and is a different phenomenon.

Q: A 25-year-old with multiple sexual partners is considering PrEP. Besides HIV testing, what additional evaluation is recommended before starting?

A. HLA-B*5701 genotype · B. Tropism assay · C. Bone density scan · D. HIV genotype · E. Baseline renal function + pregnancy testing

Answer — E

E. Baseline renal function and pregnancy testing — tenofovir affects kidney function (proximal tubule toxicity, Fanconi syndrome), and pregnancy can be a contraindication.

A — HLA-B*5701 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity, and abacavir is not used in PrEP. B — a tropism assay establishes eligibility for a CCR5 antagonist (maraviroc). C — a DEXA scan documents baseline bone density but is not the required pre-PrEP evaluation. D — genotype detects resistance mutations. Also screen for hepatitis B, since stopping tenofovir/emtricitabine can let it rebound.

Section 20 · Laboratory foundations

Inside the Analyzer — What Is Measured and What Is Calculated

Three numbers on the complete blood count are measured. The rest are arithmetic. Knowing which is which explains almost every artefact you will ever be handed.

Abbreviations used in this section CBC complete blood count — the standard automated panel · RBC red blood cell, also called an erythrocyte · WBC white blood cell, also called a leukocyte · Hgb hemoglobin, in grams per decilitre · Hct hematocrit, the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells · MCV mean corpuscular volume — average red cell size · MCH mean corpuscular hemoglobin — average hemoglobin mass per cell · MCHC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin density inside the cell · RDW red cell distribution width — how variable the cell sizes are · MPV mean platelet volume · SD standard deviation · SLS sodium lauryl sulfate — the cyanide-free hemoglobin reagent · PLT-F the fluorescent platelet channel · EDTA ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid — the lavender-top anticoagulant · fL femtolitre (10−15 L) · pg picogram · nm nanometre · TAT turnaround time · CD41 / CD61 platelet glycoproteins IIb and IIIa, the flow cytometry reference markers
🔑 The three measured values — everything else is derived

The analyzer physically measures the red cell count, the MCV (both by impedance) and the hemoglobin (photometrically). The hematocrit, MCH, MCHC and RDW are all calculated from those three.

That single fact is the reason artefacts cascade. Corrupt one measured value and every number derived from it goes wrong at the same time — which is exactly what makes an impossible MCHC such a reliable alarm bell in Section 22.

The specimen — what the laboratory will accept

  1. Fresh whole blood in EDTA. The lavender-top tube. Ideal within 3 hours of collection, acceptable within 8 hours; refrigerated samples beyond that may degrade.
  2. Invert the tube several times. EDTA is sprayed on the inside surfaces of the tube, including near the top. Blood that simply runs to the bottom never meets the full dose of anticoagulant, and partial clotting follows.
  3. No clots and no clumps. A clot sequesters platelets and some white and red cells with them, so those cells never reach the aperture and the counts come back falsely low — an artefact that reads as a disease.
  4. Citrate is the fallback for platelets. A blue-top tube may be used when EDTA-dependent platelet clumping is suspected. This is the workaround that reappears in Section 22.
🧠 Two tubes, one principle, opposite requirements

The CBC uses EDTA, which binds calcium irreversibly — fine, because the analyzer only needs to count intact cells. Coagulation testing uses sodium citrate, which binds calcium reversibly so the laboratory can add calcium back and restart clotting on demand (Section 26). Same principle, opposite requirement, different tube. Getting them the wrong way round makes both tests uninterpretable.

One practical footnote on tube brands: in the laboratory's own correlation study, MCV, RDW and hematocrit ran 1–2% higher in one manufacturer's tube than another's. Not clinically significant in isolation — but when you are trending a value over time, such as an MCV rising on iron therapy, use the same tube type and remove the variable.

Four measurement principles cover the whole panel ★ HY

Impedance — the Coulter principle

counting and sizing

Cells in a conductive fluid are drawn through a narrow aperture; each cell crossing changes the electrical impedance. Each pulse is one cell (the count) and pulse height is that cell's volume (the size). Gives RBC + MCV, platelets + MPV, and the total white count.

Flow cytometry

the differential

Separates cells by forward scatter (size) against side scatter (complexity and granularity). Those two axes are what let the machine tell a lymphocyte from a neutrophil — the white cell differential comes from here, not from impedance.

SLS photometry at 555 nm

hemoglobin

Sodium lauryl sulfate lyses red and white cells, the heme is oxidised, SLS binds it into a stable coloured complex, and absorbance is read at 555 nm — a wavelength chosen to minimise interference from turbidity. Cyanide-free, unlike the older cyanmethemoglobin reference method.

Fluorescence — the PLT-F channel

difficult platelet counts

Stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with oxazine and counts by fluorescent intensity — identifying platelets by what they contain rather than how big they are. Correlates with CD41/CD61 flow cytometry; especially useful below 50 × 10³/µL.

🪝 Memory hook — the machine decides what a cell is almost entirely from its size

There is more than one aperture, each sized for its population: a small pore for platelets, a mid-size one for red cells, a larger one for white cells. So anything that is the wrong size for its identity is counted as the wrong thing, and that one idea generates most of Section 22:

Too small → counted as a platelet. Schistocytes, microcytes and white cell fragments falsely raise the platelet count. Too big to be a platelet → missed. Platelet clumps and giant platelets falsely lower it.

The formulas, and the ranges to carry ★ HY

IndexMeasured or calculatedFormulaNormal adult rangeWhat it means
RBC — red cell countMeasured (impedance)—3.5–5.5 × 10⁶/µLHow many cells there are
Hgb — hemoglobinMeasured (SLS, 555 nm)—14–18 g/dL male; 12–16 g/dL femaleOxygen-carrying capacity — the number that defines anemia
MCV — mean corpuscular volumeMeasured (pulse height)—80–100 fL; lower in childrenAverage red cell size — the first branch of the anemia algorithm
Hct — hematocritCalculated(RBC × MCV) / 1040–50% male; 36–48% femaleProportion of blood volume that is red cells
MCH — mean corpuscular hemoglobinCalculated(Hgb / RBC) × 1026–34 pg/cellAverage amount of hemoglobin per cell
MCHC — mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentrationCalculated(Hgb / Hct) × 10031–37 g/dLHemoglobin density — a concentration, and therefore bounded by physics
RDW — red cell distribution widthCalculatedSD of volume / MCV11.4–14.5Variation in cell size — the width of the impedance curve
ReticulocytesMeasured (RNA stain)—0.8–4%Is the marrow responding? The branch point in the normocytic column
🧠 MCH versus MCHC — the pair students reliably confuse

MCH is an amount; MCHC is a concentration. A cell can contain little hemoglobin because it is small (low MCH, normal MCHC), or because it is underfilled for its size (low MCHC — true hypochromia).

Because MCHC is a density it has a physical ceiling, and that is what makes it the best artefact detector on the panel. A reported MCHC above about 37 g/dL is usually impossible and points at a laboratory interference rather than a disease. The one genuine exception is hereditary spherocytosis (Section 8), where the cells really are hyperdense — there, a high MCHC is a clue, not an error.

🪝 The rule of three — and why breaking it is itself a finding

Hematocrit ≈ 3 × hemoglobin. Hemoglobin 10 g/dL should give a hematocrit near 30%. The qualifier that makes it usable: this holds only when the MCV is normal, because the two are linked through cell size.

So a hemoglobin and hematocrit that do not fit the rule of three is not merely an oddity — it points either at abnormal red cell size or at one of the interferences in Section 22. The same check appears in Section 2; here you can see exactly why it works.

Reticulocytes and nucleated red cells — what a nucleus is for

🧠 Why a red cell has a nucleus at all, and why losing it matters

A red cell is born with a nucleus because it needs one to manufacture its hemoglobin. Once fully loaded, the nucleus has no further use and gets in the way, so the cell ejects it. A reticulocyte is the stage just after that — no nucleus, but still carrying leftover RNA, which is what the reticulocyte stain detects. A mature red cell has neither.

Three consequences worth carrying:

  1. A nucleated red cell in the blood is a cell released before it was finished. Either the marrow is under stress and rushing output, or something is taking over the marrow and forcing cells out — fibrosis, metastasis. Either way it needs explaining (Section 24).
  2. The analyzer counts nucleated red cells as white cells unless it corrects for them, because it is looking for nuclei. That is one of the interferences in Section 22.
  3. G6PD deficiency behaves the way it does because of this. With no nucleus, the G6PD a red cell carries at birth is all it will ever have — it cannot make more, so a deficient cell runs out of oxidant protection partway through its life (Section 8).
🔑 The immature platelet fraction is the reticulocyte count for platelets

Same logic, different lineage. Its clinical use is monitoring engraftment after a stem cell or marrow transplant: the platelet count is still low, but if immature platelets start appearing, the new marrow has begun producing — and the actual count will start to rise in two or three days. Days of warning you would not otherwise have.

Reticulocyte is to red cell as immature platelet fraction is to platelet. Both answer “is the marrow producing?” before the mature count moves.

The anemia algorithm, as the laboratory draws it ★ HY

Start with a low hemoglobin, split on the MCV, and then — in the normocytic column only — split again on the reticulocyte count. This is the same tree as Section 3, laid out the way the analyzer hands it to you.

MCV < 80 fL · microcyticMCV 80–100 · normocytic, low reticsMCV 80–100 · normocytic, high reticsMCV > 100 fL · macrocytic
Iron deficiency
Thalassemia — may show an increased RBC count
Hemoglobin E variant
Metal toxicity
(chronic disease)
(sideroblastic anemia)		 Renal failure
Chronic disease
Sideroblastic anemia
Hypoendocrine states
Aplastic anemia
“Mixed” deficiency		 Hemolysis
Recovery from an insult
Hemoglobinopathies

Membranopathies		 Megaloblastic anemia
Alcohol
