Complications of a prothrombotic state ★ HY

Venous thromboembolism

the common endpoint

Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The DVT is painful; the PE can kill. Post-thrombotic syndrome follows recurrent or extensive leg thrombosis.

Thrombosis at unusual sites

the red flag

Mesenteric, upper extremity, cerebral venous sinus. Unusual location is itself an indication to investigate for thrombophilia.

Pregnancy morbidity

antiphospholipid syndrome

Recurrent early loss, fetal death at or beyond 10 weeks, or premature birth before 34 weeks from eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency (Section 30).

Purpura fulminans

homozygous protein C / S

Neonatal dermal microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis — occluded capillaries rupture and blood leaks out. The purpura is a consequence of clotting.

Warfarin-induced skin necrosis

the iatrogenic version

Protein C falls before the procoagulant factors do, so the first days of warfarin are transiently more prothrombotic. Classically in patients with underlying protein C deficiency.

Venous limb gangrene

warfarin alone in HIT

The same protein C mechanism in a patient who is already thrombosing. This is why warfarin alone is prohibited in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia ★ HY

⚠️ The counterintuitive core of HIT

HIT is a prothrombotic state. The platelet count falls, but the danger is thrombosis, not bleeding — new venous and arterial clots at a ratio of roughly 4:1 venous to arterial. Every management error below follows from forgetting this.

🧠 Why it takes 5–14 days, and why past HIT closes off the whole class

The delay is an immune delay. Heparin binds platelets and forms a complex with platelet factor 4; the patient's immune system then has to recognise that complex and manufacture antibodies against it, which takes 5–14 days. The antibody then binds platelets and activates them — which is why the count falls (they are being consumed into clots) and why the patient clots rather than bleeds.

That also explains the variants: with pre-existing antibody from exposure in the past 100 days there is no immunisation delay, so onset is within hours. A few patients present days after heparin has been stopped — easy to miss, because the drug is already gone.

And the consequence for the future: once a patient has had HIT, low-molecular-weight heparin and fondaparinux are closed off too. They are structurally related and the existing antibody can cross-react. A lower risk of causing HIT is not the same as being safe once the antibody exists.

🔑 The 4T score — a decision rule, not a description
Criterion2 points1 point0 points
Thrombocytopenia> 50% fall, or nadir 20–100 × 10⁹/L30–50% fall, or nadir 10–20 × 10⁹/LFall < 30%, or nadir < 10 × 10⁹/L
Timing of the fallClear onset days 5–10; or < 1 day if heparin exposure within the past 100 daysConsistent with immunisation but not clear, or onset after day 10Fall too early, without recent heparin exposure
Thrombosis or other sequelaeNew thrombosis; skin necrosis; post-heparin-bolus acute systemic reactionProgressive or recurrent thrombosis; erythematous skin lesions; suspected but unproven thrombosisNone
oTher cause for thrombocytopeniaNo other cause evidentPossible other cause evidentDefinite other cause present

6–8 = high · 4–5 = intermediate · 0–3 = low pre-test probability. The score exists to tell you whether to test at all:

High (6–8) → treat as HIT. Stop the heparin, start an alternative. Do not wait for a result. Low (0–3) → do not send the test. It is not HIT, and a false positive will cause harm — plenty of people carry the anti-PF4 antibody without having HIT, and an indiscriminate assay generates positives that force you to stop heparin in patients who never had the disease. Intermediate (4–5) → this is where testing actually helps decide.

🪝 How to read the result once you have it

Negative is genuinely useful. The anti-heparin/PF4 immunoassay is very sensitive, so a negative result essentially rules HIT out.

Positive leaves you stuck. It is not specific, so you must treat as HIT while sending the serotonin release assay — a functional test that takes the patient's platelets, adds heparin, and measures whether serotonin is released. It is complex and run only in reference laboratories, so the answer is not quick. Which is precisely why clinical impression is the most important element, listed ahead of any assay.

Read honestly: laboratory testing does not exclude a diagnosis of HIT, but the negative predictive value approaches 100% when both the serotonin release assay and the PF4 assay are negative. And positive results alone do not mean the thrombocytopenia can be attributed solely to heparin — anti-PF4 antibodies are common in hospitalised patients. Co-existing causes must be considered.

⚠️ Treatment — and the three errors the lecture names explicitly

HIT is a hypercoagulable state, but you cannot use any heparin compound and you cannot use warfarin. Institute an alternative antithrombotic: argatroban or lepirudin (direct thrombin inhibitors).

  1. Do not use warfarin alone — associated with gangrene. Warfarin drops protein C before it drops the procoagulant factors, transiently deepening the prothrombotic state in a patient who is already thrombosing. Venous limb gangrene is the result.
  2. Do not switch to low-molecular-weight heparin — the antibody cross-reacts.
  3. Do not stop anticoagulation altogether. The instinct to stop everything because the platelets are low is exactly wrong.
🧠 The tail — why aPTT monitors unfractionated heparin but not the low-molecular-weight ones

Heparin is a chain of sugars, and it comes in different lengths — much like von Willebrand factor multimers.

To inactivate thrombin, antithrombin and thrombin must be bridged together, and it is the heparin molecule's long tail that provides that bridge. Only a long chain can do it. To inactivate factor 10a, no bridge is needed — antithrombin does it well on its own once heparin has activated it. A short chain is enough.

AgentAnti-thrombin effectAnti-factor-10a effectSo monitor with
Unfractionated heparin (long tail)StrongStrongaPTT works — it senses the thrombin effect. Anti-Xa also valid
LMWH, fondaparinux (short)WeakStrongAnti-factor 10a only — the aPTT has little to detect

Targets: unfractionated heparin aPTT 1.5–2.5× normal or anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 U/mL; low-molecular-weight heparin generally needs no monitoring, but if measured, anti-Xa 0.5–1.0 U/mL twice-daily dosing, 1.0–2.0 U/mL once daily. A practice note: anti-factor 10a has largely replaced the aPTT even for unfractionated heparin in many laboratories, so a modern chart saying “therapeutic heparin level” usually means the anti-Xa result.

Risk stratification — the numbers that decide duration ★ HY

🔑 Recurrence risk in the first year, by the circumstances of the clot
Situation at the time of thrombosisExampleRecurrence risk in the first year
Major transient risk factorProlonged bedrest in hospital, surgery3%
Minor reversible risk factorOral contraceptive, long airplane trip5%
Unprovoked VTE, or a persistent risk factorNo identifiable trigger; ongoing malignancy10%

This is the core of the objective: determine which risk factors were present at the time of the thrombosis, because that — more than any genetic test — predicts recurrence and therefore therapy length.

Thrombophilic defectAnnual risk of first DVTRelative risk vs controlsRisk of recurrence
Antithrombin · protein C · protein S deficiency1.52–1.90%15–19×At 5 years 40%; at 10 years 55%
Factor V Leiden · prothrombin G20210A · high factor 80.34–0.49%3–5×At 5 years 11%; at 10 years 25%
High factor 9 · high factor 11 · high TAFI · hyperhomocysteinemiaNot independent risk factors for venous thrombosis — the risk is associated with high factor 8
🪝 The clinically important asymmetry: common ≠ dangerous

Compare the two rows. Losing a brake (antithrombin, protein C, protein S) gives a relative risk of 15–19×. Pushing the accelerator (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) gives only 3–5×.

Factor V Leiden is by far the most common thrombophilia and by no means the most dangerous one — which is exactly why finding it in a patient with a provoked clot rarely changes management.

When to test, and when not to ★ HY

🔑 The rule that governs all of this

Put more forcefully in the recording than on the slide: “If you're sending the test and the result doesn't impact anything you're doing, you probably didn't need to send that test.” These assays cost money and, worse, generate findings that invite unnecessary lifelong therapy.

So before sending, be able to finish this sentence: if it is positive I will <do X>; if it is negative I will <do Y>. If X and Y are the same, don't send it. The two answers that legitimately justify testing are “it will change whether or how long I anticoagulate” and “it will trigger family counselling and screening”.

When to evaluate for thrombophilia — and note how closely this list mirrors the hereditary-bleeding features in Section 27:

  • Family history of clotting.
  • Young age — under 45 years.
  • Absence of risk factors — no recent surgery, long flight, or malignancy.
  • Recurrent thromboses.
  • Unusual location — upper extremity, mesenteric vessels, cerebral venous sinus.
  • Specific paediatric scenarios — single ventricle physiology, ventricular assist device evaluation.
⚠️ Why thrombophilia testing in the acute period is unreliable
SituationEffect on testing
PregnancyAlters multiple factor and protein levels
Acute period and inflammationElevated factor 8 and fibrinogen
HeparinDecreases antithrombin III levels
WarfarinDecreases protein C and protein S levels
The thrombosis itselfAntithrombin III and proteins C and S may be consumed by the clot
Lupus anticoagulantMay be transient — hence the 12-week repeat requirement

Genetic testing is the one exception. Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A may be run at any time — DNA does not change with acute illness or drugs — and only ever need running once. It is expensive, and the answer will never change.

The recommendation for everything else: wait several months after the thrombotic episode, and if possible, off anticoagulation.

🩺 Diagnosing the clot itself — what this lecture gives you, and what it does not

This lecture supplies the pre-test probability half of the deep vein thrombosis workup: Virchow's triad, the transient/persistent/inherited risk-factor table, the dependent-site rule, and the D-dimer as a marker of clot turnover (Section 26) that rises whenever fibrin is being formed and broken down.

What it does not supply is the formal diagnostic algorithm — a validated clinical decision rule, the D-dimer's role as a rule-out in low-probability patients, compression ultrasonography, or CT pulmonary angiography for suspected embolism. That part of objective 15 is still pending a dedicated lecture, and is flagged as partial in the coverage map for that reason.

🔑 The lecture's closing summary
  • Several abnormalities increase thrombosis risk: decreased anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin, proteins C and S) and increased procoagulant proteins (mutated factor 5, prothrombin overexpression, increased factor 8).
  • Diagnosis in the acute period may be difficult.
  • Before testing for thrombophilia, consider whether the patient has other clotting risk factors — cancer, obesity, immobility.
  • A variety of blood clotting medications are available. Therapy length should be based on risk factors and risk of recurrence, not on the presence of a thrombophilia alone.

Q: A post-operative patient on unfractionated heparin has a platelet count fall from 240,000 to 85,000/µL on day 7, and develops a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the 4T score, and what are the two most important immediate actions?

Answer

4T score = 8, high probability. Thrombocytopenia: a > 50% fall with a nadir between 20 and 100 × 10⁹/L — 2 points. Timing: clear onset on day 7, within the 5–10 day window — 2 points. Thrombosis: new thrombosis — 2 points. Other cause: none evident — 2 points.

Two immediate actions: (1) stop all heparin, including flushes and heparin-bonded lines, and (2) start an alternative anticoagulant — argatroban. Send heparin–PF4 antibodies, but do not wait for the result to act.

Do not switch to low-molecular-weight heparin (cross-reactivity), do not start warfarin alone (gangrene risk from the early protein C drop), and do not simply stop anticoagulation because the platelets are low.

Q: A 28-year-old woman has a deep vein thrombosis two weeks after starting a combined oral contraceptive. Testing while she is on heparin shows a low antithrombin III level and heterozygous factor V Leiden. How should you interpret these results, and how long should she be treated?

Answer

The antithrombin result is uninterpretable. Heparin decreases antithrombin III levels, and antithrombin can also be consumed by the acute thrombosis itself. It must be repeated several months later, off anticoagulation.

The factor V Leiden result is valid, because genetic testing may be run at any time. But heterozygous factor V Leiden carries a relative risk of only 3–5× — far less than an anticoagulant-protein deficiency at 15–19× — and roughly 5% of Caucasians carry it.

Duration is set by the circumstances of the clot, not the genotype. The oral contraceptive is a minor reversible risk factor, giving about a 5% recurrence risk in the first year. Standard-duration treatment with removal of the trigger (stopping the contraceptive) is appropriate; the factor V Leiden result does not by itself justify indefinite anticoagulation.

Q: Given that roughly 25% of the general population has some thrombophilia, why is finding one in a patient with a provoked clot rarely useful?

Answer

Because a finding that common has poor specificity — with a quarter of everyone carrying something, a positive result is close to expected and does not establish causation for this clot.

More decisively, the result does not change management. Duration of anticoagulation is driven by the recurrence risk, which is set by the circumstances: 3% after a major transient risk factor, 5% after a minor reversible one, 10% for unprovoked or persistent risk. A provoked clot sits in the low-risk group whether or not factor V Leiden is present.

This is exactly why the lecture insists on asking first how a positive result will be used. If the answer is “it will not change therapy”, the remaining justification is family counselling — and that is a separate discussion, best had months later and off anticoagulation.

Q: A patient is started on low-molecular-weight heparin. The house officer orders a daily aPTT and is puzzled that it is normal. What has gone wrong, and what should be measured instead?

Answer

The aPTT is the wrong test for a low-molecular-weight heparin, and a normal result does not mean the patient is under-anticoagulated.

The mechanism is chain length. To inactivate thrombin, antithrombin and thrombin must be bridged together, and only a long heparin tail can provide that bridge. To inactivate factor 10a, no bridge is needed — a short chain is enough. So low-molecular-weight heparins have a strong anti-factor-10a effect and a weak anti-thrombin effect, and the aPTT, which senses the thrombin effect, has little to detect.

Most patients on low-molecular-weight heparin need no monitoring at all — that predictability is the point of the drug. When monitoring is genuinely indicated (pregnancy, obesity, renal impairment), measure anti-factor 10a activity: 0.5–1.0 U/mL for twice-daily dosing, 1.0–2.0 U/mL for once-daily.

Section 32 · Hematologic malignancy · the frame

The Core Construct, and the Acute Leukemia Emergencies

One idea organizes every blood cancer: a cell somewhere along the path from pluripotent stem cell to fully differentiated cell acquires a mutation — and where on that path it happens determines which disease you get, and how fast it will kill.

Abbreviations used in this section AML acute myeloid leukemia · ALL acute lymphoblastic leukemia · APL acute promyelocytic leukemia · MDS myelodysplastic syndrome · MPN myeloproliferative neoplasm · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · TLS tumour lysis syndrome · Blast an immature, undifferentiated precursor cell · Indolent slow-growing · Pluripotent stem cell the earliest marrow cell, able to become any blood cell · Progeny the descendant cells of a dividing cell · ANC absolute neutrophil count
🔑 The principal construct ★ HY

A hematopoietic cell in the bone marrow or lymph system acquires a mutation, or a series of mutations, that disrupts the differentiation and maturation of its progeny. The resulting disease depends on the maturation stage of the cell that undergoes transformation:

  • Less differentiated → AGGRESSIVE
  • More differentiated → INDOLENT

Note the phrase of its progeny. The mutated cell itself is not usually the problem — the problem is that everything descended from it is frozen at a stage where it should not be, and keeps dividing.

The map — two lineages across, differentiation stage along each ★ HY

LineageAggressive (less differentiated)IntermediateIndolent / normally differentiated
MYELOIDAcute myeloid leukemia — over 20% blastsMyelodysplastic syndrome — abnormal differentiation, a disruption in maturationPolycythemia vera · essential thrombocythemia · myelofibrosis · chronic myeloid leukemia
LYMPHOIDAcute lymphoblastic leukemia · Burkitt lymphoma · diffuse large B-cell lymphoma—Follicular lymphoma · chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma · marginal zone lymphoma · lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
PLASMA CELL——Multiple myeloma — a fully mature plasma cell

Read left to right and the tempo changes from weeks (acute leukemia) to years or decades (myeloma, follicular lymphoma).

🧠 Why myeloma sits at the far right

The plasma cell is the fully differentiated end-point of the B-cell lineage — an antibody factory and nothing else. A cancer of that cell keeps doing what plasma cells do: it makes a single antibody in enormous quantity (the monoclonal protein). It does not blast the marrow the way an acute leukemia does.

That is why multiple myeloma is a chronic disease measured in years, and why its complications — kidney failure from light chains, bone lesions, hypercalcemia — come from the product of the cell rather than from its proliferation.

The darkest corollary runs the other way: in the very least differentiated cancers you can get an acute leukemia with both myeloid and lymphoid features — transformation before the myeloid/lymphoid branch point — and the prognosis is correspondingly dismal.

🪝 Memory hook — differentiation is a one-way street

A highly specialized cell can never go back and become something else. A cancer arising early on that street therefore inherits the proliferative capacity of an undifferentiated cell. That single fact is why acute leukemias are aggressive and plasma cell disorders are chronic — and it makes the whole taxonomy predictable rather than a list to memorize.

Acute leukemia — the defining features ★ HY

  • Unregulated growth of undifferentiated cells in the marrow called blasts.
  • Cells rapidly overwhelm the marrow and spill out into the peripheral blood.
  • Diagnosis requires more than 20% blasts in the bone marrow OR the peripheral blood. Either compartment suffices. Memorize this number — it is also the line that separates myelodysplastic syndrome and chronic myeloid leukemia blast phase from acute leukemia.
  • May have a high, normal, or LOW white blood cell count at presentation. A normal white count does not exclude acute leukemia.
  • Universally present with bone marrow failure — anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia.
  • Rapidly fatal: untreated, death within 12 weeks in most cases.
🩺 The presenting vignette, and why every element points one way

A 57-year-old previously healthy woman with 3 weeks of progressive malaise and spontaneous bruising. Pulse 110, pallor, scattered ecchymoses. White cells 87,000 · hemoglobin 6.2 · platelets 45,000 · neutrophils 0.6 with 90% blasts.

The white count is enormous but she is functionally neutropenic — the cells are all blasts, which do nothing. She is anemic, thrombocytopenic and neutropenic simultaneously: trilineage marrow failure with a packed marrow, which is the signature of acute leukemia.

“Extinguish the fire” — the initial management

  1. Treat the marrow failure — transfusion support. Transfuse for hemoglobin below 7, platelets below 10,000 — or below 50,000 if actively bleeding. Identify and treat infection, which in a neutropenic patient is the thing most likely to kill them this week.
  2. Buy time — control the unchecked white cell growth. Hydroxyurea. This is cytoreduction, not cure — it holds the count down while the diagnostic workup proceeds and definitive therapy is arranged.

The two metabolic emergencies ★ HY

🩸

Disseminated intravascular coagulation

Uncontrolled intravascular consumption of clotting factors.

  • Low fibrinogen
  • High partial thromboplastin time and prothrombin time
  • Low platelets
  • Accompanied by thrombotic microangiopathy — hemolysis with schistocytes on the smear

Most strongly associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia, where it is the cause of early death.

💥

Tumour lysis syndrome

Rapid cell turnover and death releasing intracellular contents. Four derangements, each with its own treatment:

  • Hyperuricemia → renal failure. Prevention: allopurinol. Severe: rasburicase
  • Hyperphosphatemia
  • Hypocalcemia — may need calcium replacement
  • Hyperkalemia → arrhythmia. Treatment: sodium polystyrene

Watch for it in acute leukemias and aggressive lymphomas — particularly Burkitt — either spontaneously or on starting treatment.

🔑 The tumour lysis pattern in one line

Everything goes UP except calcium. Potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down — because the released phosphate binds and precipitates the calcium. If a question lists three highs and one low in a patient starting chemotherapy, this is the diagnosis.

Note the discrimination against DIC: DIC is a coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, prolonged times, schistocytes); tumour lysis is metabolic. They are both emergencies of the first week, and they are not the same problem.

🧠 Grade and stage — how they change prognosis and treatment

In hematolymphoid neoplasms, “grade” is essentially the aggressive/indolent axis of the core construct, and it inverts the usual intuition about what a bad diagnosis means:

  • High-grade / aggressive disease kills in 3–6 months untreated — but is treated with curative intent, because rapidly dividing cells are exactly what chemotherapy kills.
  • Low-grade / indolent disease is compatible with decades of life — but is not curable by standard therapy, because most cells are never cycling when the drug is present. A third of follicular lymphoma patients are never treated at all.

Stage (Ann Arbor) behaves differently in each: advanced stage drives urgency in aggressive lymphoma, while indolent lymphoma is usually stage III/IV at diagnosis and that fact alone changes nothing. Molecular findings can outweigh clinical stage entirely — a double hit lymphoma does worse than the highest clinical risk score.

Q: A patient presents with a white cell count of 87,000, of which 90% are blasts, plus anemia and thrombocytopenia. Absolute neutrophil count is 0.6. Why is this patient at high risk of infection despite a white count of 87,000?

Answer

Because blasts are non-functional. The white count measures cells, not function — the patient is functionally neutropenic with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.6 despite a hugely elevated total. Identifying and treating infection is one of the two immediate priorities, alongside transfusion support.

Q: Two days after starting induction chemotherapy, a patient has potassium 6.4, phosphate 7.1, calcium 6.8 and uric acid 14. Name the syndrome and give the treatment for each abnormality.

Answer

Tumour lysis syndrome. Hyperuricemia → allopurinol for prevention, rasburicase if severe (it degrades existing urate rather than merely blocking production); this is the abnormality that causes renal failure. Hyperkalemia → sodium polystyrene, with urgent attention because of arrhythmia risk. Hyperphosphatemia drives the hypocalcemia, which may need calcium replacement.

Q: Two patients transform at different points in the B-cell lineage. One develops Burkitt lymphoma, the other multiple myeloma. Using only the core construct, predict the difference in tempo and explain why.

Answer

Burkitt lymphoma is highly aggressive; multiple myeloma is chronic. Burkitt arises from a less differentiated B cell, which retains enormous proliferative capacity — it is one of the fastest-growing human tumours. Myeloma arises from the fully differentiated plasma cell, whose job is secretion rather than division, so the disease is measured in years and its damage comes from the monoclonal protein and light chains rather than from raw growth.

LO 51LO 87LO 43LO 92Source: Introduction to Hematologic Malignancy

Section 33 · Hematologic malignancy · myeloid, acute

Acute Myeloid Leukemia — and Its One Curable Variant

The disease you stabilize first and subtype second — except for one variant, where you must start the treatment before the diagnosis is confirmed, because the coagulopathy kills before the cytogenetics come back.

Abbreviations used in this section AML acute myeloid leukemia · APL acute promyelocytic leukemia · ATRA all-trans retinoic acid, a vitamin A derivative that forces differentiation · PML-RARA the fusion gene of t(15;17), joining the promyelocytic leukemia gene to the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene · Flow cytometry a laser-based technique identifying cell surface antigens, used to assign lineage · 7 + 3 7 days of cytarabine infusion plus 3 days of an anthracycline · Anthracycline daunorubicin or idarubicin · CR complete remission · Allo-SCT allogeneic stem cell transplant, using donor stem cells · Hypomethylating agent decitabine or azacitidine · Cytogenetics analysis of chromosome structure · Performance status a standardized measure of how much a patient can do for themselves
DomainWhat to know
DiagnosisBone marrow biopsy and aspirate showing more than 20% blasts, with myeloid cell surface antigens on flow cytometry. Flow cytometry is what assigns lineage — blast morphology alone will not
Risk factorsPrior cytotoxic chemotherapy · a history of myelodysplastic syndrome or a myeloproliferative disorder · Down syndrome. Note that two of the three are iatrogenic or antecedent hematologic disease — this is often a second cancer
Prognostic featuresAge · performance status · comorbidities · prior cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiation · antecedent myeloid disorders · cytogenetic and molecular findings. The last stratifies patients into high, intermediate and low risk — and that stratification decides who gets a transplant

Treatment — two intents, decided by fitness rather than by age alone

🎯

Curative intent — younger / fit

Induction: “7 + 3” — daunorubicin or idarubicin plus cytarabine. Requires at least a 3–4 week hospitalization. The goal is complete remission.

Consolidation: more intensive chemotherapy. Allogeneic stem cell transplant for intermediate or high risk disease.

🤝

Palliative intent — older / unfit

Hypomethylating agent — decitabine or azacitidine — with or without venetoclax.

Supportive care: transfusions, antibiotics, hospice.

The choice between columns turns on whether the patient can survive a month of marrow aplasia in hospital, not simply on a birthday.

⚠️ Acute promyelocytic leukemia — the one you must not miss ★ HY

A biologically and genetically distinct variant of acute myeloid leukemia, and the single highest-yield disease in this section.

  • Translocation t(15;17) → the PML-RARA fusion gene.
  • Severe disseminated intravascular coagulation causes early death from bleeding in unrecognized cases. The patient does not die of the leukemia — they die of hemorrhage, often within days, often before the diagnosis is confirmed.
  • Treat with all-trans retinoic acid, which does not kill the cells but forces the arrested promyelocytes to differentiate — the purest possible illustration of the core construct.
  • 90% overall survival. This transforms the most rapidly lethal leukemia into the most curable one — but only if it is recognized.

The practical rule: in a new acute leukemia with a coagulopathy, start all-trans retinoic acid on suspicion, before the cytogenetics come back. The cost of being wrong is small; the cost of waiting is a fatal bleed.

🧠 Why differentiation therapy is the perfect proof of the core construct

The lecture's central idea is that disease arises from arrested differentiation. All-trans retinoic acid does not poison the cell — it releases the block, and the promyelocytes mature into cells that then die naturally. A drug that cures a cancer without conventional cytotoxicity is only conceivable if the disease was a maturation problem in the first place.

🩺 Complications of acute leukemia — what actually kills, and when
  • Week one: infection in a functionally neutropenic patient; hemorrhage from thrombocytopenia or DIC (above all in APL); tumour lysis syndrome on starting treatment.
  • During induction: a month of profound marrow aplasia — neutropenic sepsis, transfusion dependence, mucositis.
  • Longer term: relapse; graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic transplant; and, for survivors of prior cytotoxic therapy, therapy-related AML itself as a second malignancy.

Q: A 46-year-old presents with acute leukemia, fibrinogen 80, prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time both prolonged, and platelets 22,000. What is the likely subtype, the genetic lesion, and what should be started immediately?

Answer

Acute promyelocytic leukemia. The lesion is t(15;17), producing PML-RARA. Start all-trans retinoic acid immediately, on suspicion, without waiting for confirmatory cytogenetics — because severe disseminated intravascular coagulation causes early death from bleeding in unrecognized cases. Support the coagulopathy aggressively with blood products. Recognized and treated, overall survival is 90%.

Q: A 78-year-old with heart failure and poor performance status is diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia. Why is “7 + 3” induction generally inappropriate, and what is offered instead?

Answer

Because “7 + 3” requires at least a 3–4 week hospitalization through a period of profound marrow aplasia, which an unfit patient with significant comorbidity is unlikely to survive. The palliative-intent pathway is a hypomethylating agent — decitabine or azacitidine — with or without venetoclax, plus supportive care. The decision is driven by fitness, performance status and comorbidity, not by age alone.

LO 8LO 42LO 43LO 63Source: Introduction to Hematologic Malignancy

Section 34 · Hematologic malignancy · myeloid, chronic

Myelodysplastic Syndrome and Chronic Myeloid Leukemia

A factory that builds defective cells, and the greatest success story in oncology — separated on the map by whether differentiation is abnormal or normal.

Abbreviations used in this section MDS myelodysplastic syndrome · Dysplastic abnormally formed · Cytopenia a low blood cell count · Epigenetic altering gene expression without changing the DNA sequence, chiefly by methylation · CML chronic myeloid leukemia · t(9;22) a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 · BCR-ABL the fusion gene it creates, encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase · Philadelphia chromosome the shortened chromosome 22 resulting from that translocation · TKI tyrosine kinase inhibitor · T315I the gatekeeper point mutation causing resistance to most tyrosine kinase inhibitors · Constitutively active permanently switched on, independent of normal regulation · LAP leukocyte alkaline phosphatase

Myelodysplastic syndrome — the defining paradox

🔑 Dysplastic and ineffective blood cell production

The marrow is cellular — often hypercellular — yet the patient is cytopenic, because the cells being produced are structurally abnormal and die before they leave, or shortly after. Production is not reduced; it is wasted.

MDS occupies the middle box of the map: not undifferentiated like acute myeloid leukemia, not normally differentiated like the myeloproliferative neoplasms, but abnormally differentiated.

DomainDetail
Clinical presentationAnemia · thrombocytopenia · neutropenia — any or all lineages. Anemia is usually the first and the most prominent
PathophysiologyEpigenetic changes — which is precisely why hypomethylating drugs are the disease-directed treatment
Causes of death30% progress to acute myeloid leukemia. 50% die of bleeding or infection — that is, of the cytopenias themselves
TreatmentSupportive: transfusions, growth factors, antibiotics. Disease-directed: hypomethylating drugs (azacitidine, decitabine). Curative: allogeneic stem cell transplant — the only one
⚠️ What kills most patients with MDS is counter-intuitive

50% die of bleeding or infection — complications of the cytopenias. Only 30% die from progression to acute myeloid leukemia. The feared outcome, leukemic transformation, is the less common one.

🧠 The mechanism-to-drug link

The pathophysiology is epigenetic — genes are silenced by methylation rather than deleted by mutation. A hypomethylating agent removes that silencing and lets normal differentiation resume. This is the same drug class used for unfit AML, which makes sense given that MDS and AML are two points on one continuum separated by the 20% blast line.

Chronic myeloid leukemia — the targeted-therapy paradigm ★ HY

🔑 Definition and the defining lesion — know all three names

Unregulated growth of myeloid cells in the marrow and their accumulation in the blood.

t(9;22) (the translocation) → BCR-ABL (the fusion gene and protein) → the Philadelphia chromosome (the resulting derivative chromosome 22). The fusion protein is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase — permanently switched on — which is exactly why a small molecule that blocks its active site works so well.

Presentation: often asymptomatic, frequently found on a routine blood count. Neutrophilia, basophilia, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis — the whole myeloid series is elevated. Basophilia is the distinctive one; few other conditions raise basophils. Plus splenomegaly.

PhaseDefining features
Chronic phaseUsually asymptomatic. 85% of patients present here
Accelerated phaseAny of: persistent or increasing high white cell count unresponsive to therapy · persistent or increasing splenomegaly · persistent thrombocytosis above 1,000 × 10⁹/L unresponsive to therapy · persistent thrombocytopenia below 100 × 10⁹/L unrelated to therapy · at least 20% basophils in the peripheral blood · 10–19% blasts · any new clonal chromosomal abnormality arising during therapy
Blast phaseMore than 20% blasts in the marrow or blood — i.e. it has become an acute leukemia
🧠 Two numbers, two meanings — do not confuse them

In accelerated phase, 10–19% BLASTS and at least 20% BASOPHILS are two separate criteria that both involve a number near 20. Blasts above 20% means blast phase (acute leukemia). Basophils at or above 20% means accelerated phase. Read the cell type before the number.

🔑 CML versus a leukemoid reaction — the discrimination ★ HY

Both present with a strikingly high neutrophil count. The features that separate them:

FeatureChronic myeloid leukemiaLeukemoid reaction
Molecular geneticst(9;22) / BCR-ABL positive — the definitive testNegative
BasophiliaPresent — the distinctive findingAbsent
EosinophiliaPresentAbsent
Underlying causeClonal neoplasm — no triggerA driving stimulus: severe infection, inflammation, tissue necrosis, corticosteroids
SpleenSplenomegaly typicalUsually normal
SmearWhole myeloid series, all maturation stages, including blastsMature neutrophils with toxic granulation and Döhle bodies, left shift without blasts
Leukocyte alkaline phosphataseLowHigh

The single most useful move is to send for BCR-ABL. Everything else is supportive; the molecular result is diagnostic.

Treatment tierAgents
First generationImatinib — the drug that proved targeted therapy could work
Second generationNilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib
ResistanceThe T315I gatekeeper mutation blocks binding of the earlier agents. Treat with ponatinib or omacetaxine
Treatment-free remissionSelected patients in deep, sustained molecular response can discontinue therapy under monitoring
🔑 The prognosis numbers — memorize the contrast

Before tyrosine kinase inhibitors: median survival 2–5 years. After: 95% alive at 10 years. A fatal disease converted into a chronic one by a single oral tablet — the paradigm case for molecularly targeted therapy in all of oncology.

Q: A 74-year-old has hemoglobin 8.1, platelets 90,000, neutrophils 1.1, and a hypercellular marrow with dysplastic changes and 8% blasts. What is the diagnosis, and what single number would change it?

Answer

Myelodysplastic syndrome — cytopenias with a cellular, dysplastic marrow: ineffective production. The number that would change the diagnosis is the blast percentage: more than 20% would make this acute myeloid leukemia. At 8% it remains MDS, with a 30% lifetime risk of progression.

Q: A patient with known chronic myeloid leukemia now has 24% basophils and 14% blasts in the peripheral blood. What phase is this?

Answer

Accelerated phase. Both findings are accelerated-phase criteria: at least 20% basophils and 10–19% blasts. It is not blast phase, which requires more than 20% blasts — at 14% the patient has not crossed that line. The distinction matters because blast phase is treated as an acute leukemia.

Q: A patient on imatinib loses their response. Molecular testing shows a T315I mutation. What now?

Answer

Ponatinib or omacetaxine. T315I is the gatekeeper mutation conferring resistance to imatinib and to the second-generation agents (nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib). Switching within those generations will not help — it requires the specific agents active against T315I.

LO 75LO 76LO 70Source: Introduction to Hematologic Malignancy

Section 35 · Hematologic malignancy · myeloid, chronic

The Myeloproliferative Neoplasms — Polycythemia Vera, Essential Thrombocythemia, Myelofibrosis

Three diseases, one pathway. All are driven by JAK2/STAT mutations, all produce normally differentiated cells in excess, and all can transform into one another or into acute leukemia. Their shared clinical danger is thrombosis, not marrow failure.

Abbreviations used in this section MPN myeloproliferative neoplasm · PV polycythemia vera · ET essential thrombocythemia · MF myelofibrosis · JAK2 Janus kinase 2 — the signalling kinase mutated in most myeloproliferative neoplasms · STAT signal transducer and activator of transcription — the downstream partner of JAK2 · Aquagenic pruritus itching triggered by contact with water, classically after a hot shower · Erythromelalgia episodic burning pain with redness and warmth in the extremities · Phlebotomy therapeutic removal of blood to lower the hematocrit · Hyperviscosity sludging of blood from excessive cell mass or protein · Splanchnic relating to the abdominal viscera — portal, mesenteric and splenic veins
🧠 What links the three

The JAK2/STAT pathway normally transmits growth-factor signals into the nucleus. A JAK2 mutation leaves it signalling continuously, so the marrow behaves as though it is being permanently told to produce — but the cells it makes are normal, mature and functional.

That is why these patients are not infected or bleeding from failure; they are clotting from excess. It is also why JAK2 testing appears in the thrombophilia workup for splanchnic vein thrombosis — an unexplained portal or mesenteric vein clot can be the first sign of one of these diseases.

Polycythemia vera

🌡️

Presentation

Inflammatory symptoms: night sweats · aquagenic pruritus (itching after a hot shower — highly characteristic) · erythromelalgia (burning red painful extremities) · bone pain · symptomatic splenomegaly · malaise · weight loss.

Thrombosis — arterial and venous. Risk factors: prior thrombosis · age over 60 · white cells above 11,000 · hematocrit above 45 · platelets above 400,000.

Hyperviscosity: headaches, disequilibrium.

💉

Treatment and transformation

Phlebotomy to a target hematocrit: men below 45, women below 42.

Hydroxyurea · aspirin or anticoagulation · ruxolitinib for refractory disease.

Transformation: 10% progress to post-polycythemia vera myelofibrosis; 1% develop acute myeloid leukemia.

🩺 The presentation to watch for

35-year-olds who never see a doctor and present with a heart attack — because they have this disease. A myocardial infarction or stroke in a young person with a high hematocrit or platelet count should prompt thought about a myeloproliferative neoplasm. These are among the few hematologic conditions causing arterial as well as venous thrombosis.

Essential thrombocythemia

DomainDetail
Risk stratificationOnly two factors: history of thrombosis and age over 60. Simple, and worth memorizing because it is so short
TreatmentHydroxyurea. Goal: reduce thrombosis risk — not to normalize a number for its own sake
Transformation4% lifetime risk of transformation to myelofibrosis

Myelofibrosis — the one with the worst prognosis

⚠️ The MPN that ends in marrow failure

Two components of presentation:

  • Symptom burden: bone pain, malaise, night sweats, weight loss, fevers. The symptom burden itself is a treatment indication.
  • Pancytopenia — as the marrow is replaced by fibrous tissue it stops producing. Unlike polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia, this disease ends in marrow failure.

Ruxolitinib — for intermediate-2 and high risk disease. It improves symptoms AND survival, but does NOT improve the cytopenias. That caveat is the examinable part. Allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only curative-intent treatment.

🪝 Memory hook — three diseases, three excesses, three treatments

All JAK2-driven. PV: red cell excess → phlebotomy. ET: platelet excess → hydroxyurea. MF: marrow fibrosis and PANCYTOPENIA → ruxolitinib (helps symptoms and survival, not counts). The first two are diseases of too many cells; the third is the one where the marrow finally gives out.

Q: A 58-year-old reports intense itching after hot showers, burning red hands, and headaches. Hematocrit is 58%. Diagnosis, pathway, and immediate treatment?

Answer

Polycythemia vera. Aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia are the two characteristic symptoms; the headaches reflect hyperviscosity. Driven by the JAK2/STAT pathway. Immediate treatment is phlebotomy to a hematocrit below 45 in men (below 42 in women), plus aspirin, with hydroxyurea if higher risk. Long term, 10% progress to post-PV myelofibrosis and 1% to acute myeloid leukemia.

Q: A patient with high-risk myelofibrosis has debilitating night sweats and pancytopenia. What does ruxolitinib offer, and what will it not do?

Answer

Ruxolitinib is indicated for intermediate-2 and high risk disease and improves both symptoms and survival. Critically, it does NOT improve the cytopenias — the pancytopenia will persist and may worsen. The only curative-intent treatment is allogeneic stem cell transplant.

Q: A 41-year-old presents with portal vein thrombosis and no other risk factor. Which hematologic test belongs in the workup, and why?

Answer

JAK2 mutation testing. An unexplained splanchnic (portal, mesenteric or splenic) vein thrombosis can be the first manifestation of a myeloproliferative neoplasm, sometimes before the blood counts are obviously abnormal — because the disease produces a prothrombotic state through normally differentiated but excessive cells. This is why JAK2 sits in the thrombophilia panel for splanchnic clots specifically.

LO 44LO 45LO 52LO 53LO 27LO 59LO 60Source: Introduction to Hematologic Malignancy

Section 36 · Hematologic malignancy · lymphoid

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia and the Lymphomas

The central paradox of lymphoma: the aggressive diseases are the curable ones, because rapidly dividing cells are exactly what chemotherapy kills — and the indolent ones, which patients live with for decades, are not.

Abbreviations used in this section ALL acute lymphoblastic leukemia · DLBCL diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · FL follicular lymphoma · MZL marginal zone lymphoma · MALT mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue · LPL lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, also called Waldenström macroglobulinemia · MCL mantle cell lymphoma · CLL / SLL chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma · HL Hodgkin lymphoma · B symptoms night sweats, weight loss and fever · IPI International Prognostic Index · R-CHOP rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin (hydroxydaunorubicin), vincristine (Oncovin), prednisone · ECOG a 0–5 performance-status scale · LDH lactate dehydrogenase · FISH fluorescence in situ hybridization · BTK Bruton tyrosine kinase · CAR-T chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy · BiTE bispecific T-cell engager · EBV Epstein-Barr virus · ESR erythrocyte sedimentation rate

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia — precursor B and T ★ HY

DomainDetail
EpidemiologyThe most common childhood malignancy. Bimodal peak: 2–5 years, and over 50. 85% precursor B-cell; 15% T-cell
Clinical findingsLymphadenopathy · splenomegaly · central nervous system involvement. These three extramedullary features are what distinguish it clinically from AML — ALL leaves the marrow and colonizes lymphoid tissue and the meninges, which is why treatment includes CNS prophylaxis
BCR-ABL positive B-cell diseaseA subset carries BCR-ABL — the same fusion as chronic myeloid leukemia — and responds to oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Historically the worst-prognosis group, transformed by targeted therapy
Prognosis by ageChildren: over 90% survival. Adolescents and young adults: 50–70%. Older adults: 30%. The same disease name, three very different diseases
🧠 Why the age gradient is so steep — favorable and unfavorable prognostic factors

It is not simply that children tolerate chemotherapy better. The biology differs by age: adult ALL is enriched for adverse cytogenetics — including BCR-ABL — while childhood disease is enriched for favourable ones. Add reduced tolerance of intensive protocols in older adults and the survival gap widens from over 90% to 30%.

Favourable in childhood leukemia: age 2–5 years (the peak incidence group does best), precursor-B immunophenotype, favourable cytogenetics, low presenting white count, and rapid clearance of blasts with good early response to induction. Unfavourable: infancy or adolescence/adulthood, T-cell disease, BCR-ABL or other adverse cytogenetics, high presenting white count, CNS involvement, and slow early response with persistent measurable residual disease.

Aggressive B-cell lymphomas — diffuse large B-cell and Burkitt

🔑 The defining trade-off

Often highly symptomatic on presentation. Death in 3–6 months without treatment. Treatment intent: CURE. Also: watch for tumour lysis syndrome, for exactly the same reason the disease is curable.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presents as a rapidly growing mass, often with B symptoms, and may have central nervous system involvement. First line is R-CHOP. Relapsed or refractory disease: chemoimmunotherapy, allogeneic stem cell transplant, CAR-T cell therapy, or bispecific T-cell engagers.

International Prognostic Index — adverse factor (1 point each)
Age over 60
Serum lactate dehydrogenase above normal
ECOG performance status of 2 or more
Ann Arbor stage III or IV
More than 1 extranodal disease site
IPI scoreOverall survival
0 or 181%
269%
353%
4 or 550%
Double hit lymphomaApproximately 30%
⚠️ Double hit lymphoma does worse than the worst clinical score

An IPI of 4 or 5 gives 50% overall survival. Double hit lymphoma — a balanced translocation placing MYC adjacent to BCL2 or BCL6 — gives approximately 30%. Molecular biology outweighs the clinical index here, which is exactly why every new diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is tested for MYC rearrangement with BCL2 or BCL6.

Burkitt lymphoma: highly aggressive, any age, associated with immune deficiency (HIV, allogeneic transplant), carrying t(8;14). Survival with chemoimmunotherapy: children 90%, adults 60–70%.

Indolent B-cell lymphomas ★ HY

🔑 Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma — one disease, two names

A mature B-cell neoplasm. In the marrow and blood → chronic lymphocytic leukemia. In the lymph nodes and spleen → small lymphocytic lymphoma. A patient may have either or both. It is the same disease regardless of presentation.

Diagnostic immunophenotype: CD5+, CD10−, CD20+, CD23+. Usually found as an incidental lymphocytosis on routine bloods.

Risk stratification: FISH — 13q deletion favorable; trisomy 12 or negative intermediate; 17p and 11q deletion high risk. IgVH mutated = favorable (counter-intuitive — here mutation is the good result). TP53 unfavorable.

🧠 The CD5-positive B cell is the diagnostic oddity

CD5 is normally a T-cell marker. A B-cell neoplasm (CD20+) that also expresses CD5 is distinctly unusual, and only two important diseases do it: chronic lymphocytic leukemia / SLL and mantle cell lymphoma. The discriminator is CD23: positive in CLL, negative in mantle cell — and mantle cell carries t(11;14) with cyclin D1 overexpression.

Indications for treating CLL — and note that a rising lymphocyte count on its own is not one of them: pancytopenia · bulky lymphadenopathy · severe symptoms (malaise, weight loss, night sweats) · threatened end organ function. Treatments: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, pirtobrutinib), venetoclax (BCL-2), PI3K inhibitors, anti-CD20 antibodies. 17p deletion → use a BTK or BCL-2 inhibitor, because this group responds poorly to chemoimmunotherapy. Richter transformation to large cell lymphoma occurs in 2–9% and is usually fatal.

⚠️ The paraneoplastic syndromes of CLL — and the trap

A disease of dysregulated B cells produces problems of antibody function, quite separately from tumour bulk: autoimmune hemolytic anemia · immune thrombocytopenia · hypogammaglobulinemia → recurrent sinopulmonary infections, treated with intravenous immunoglobulin.

The trap: a falling hemoglobin in CLL may be autoimmune hemolysis rather than marrow infiltration — a completely different treatment. Check a direct Coombs test.

Indolent entityWhat defines itTreatment note
Follicular lymphomaUsually asymptomatic lymphadenopathy, usually advanced stage at diagnosis — which in indolent disease does not carry the urgency it does in aggressive disease. Often months to decades before first treatmentTreat for B symptoms, cytopenias or end organ dysfunction. Median progression-free survival after chemoimmunotherapy 5–8 years. Transformation to large cell lymphoma: 30% over 10 years
Nodal marginal zone lymphomaAssociated with chronic hepatitis CAntiviral therapy may cure the lymphoma
Extranodal MZL (MALT)Stomach, intestine, salivary and lacrimal gland, thyroid, breast. Associated with Helicobacter pylori, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroiditis, Sjögren syndrome, lupusEradicating H. pylori in gastric MALT can cure the cancer
Splenic MZL—Splenectomy
Mantle cell lymphomat(11;14) → cyclin D1. Rare, twice as common in men, median age 68. 90% gastrointestinal involvement. Neither comfortably aggressive nor indolent“Aggressive and everyone relapses.” Counter-intuitively, leukemic phase only is the LOW risk group (often SOX11); high risk = symptomatic, 17p deletion, blastoid variant, raised LDH, high proliferation index
🧠 The lymphoma you can treat with an antibiotic

Marginal zone lymphoma often arises in the setting of chronic antigenic stimulation — remove the driver and the lymphoma may regress. Gastric MALT with proven H. pylori: eradication alone can cure it. Nodal MZL with active hepatitis C: antiviral therapy may resolve it. These are the clearest examples in oncology of a malignancy driven by chronic inflammation rather than by an intrinsic genetic lesion alone.

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia)

⚠️ An indolent lymphoma whose complications come from a protein

Presentation: plasmacytic differentiation · MYD88 mutation · advanced diffuse lymphadenopathy · cytopenias · an IgM monoclonal protein. Every major complication follows from the fact that the paraprotein is IgM — a large pentameric molecule:

  • Hyperviscosity syndrome — vertigo, blurred vision, headache, nystagmus, ataxia; severe: stroke, coma, delirium. Treatment: EMERGENT PLASMAPHERESIS.
  • Neuropathy — classically slowly progressive, ascending, sensorimotor.
  • Cold agglutinin autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
  • Cryoglobulinemia — Raynaud phenomenon, urticaria, purpura, acral cyanosis, tissue necrosis.
  • Bleeding and coagulopathy — the IgM paraprotein interferes with fibrin polymerization. A patient who both clots and bleeds.

Watch for the IgM “flare” during initial treatment — IgM can rise transiently when therapy begins, worsening viscosity just as you start to help.

🧠 Why IgM and not IgG causes hyperviscosity

IgM forms a pentamer — five antibody units joined together. That makes it a very large molecule that stays in the intravascular space and raises viscosity dramatically at concentrations an IgG paraprotein would tolerate. The same bulk explains the interference with fibrin polymerization that causes bleeding, and the cold agglutinin behaviour. One molecular property explains four clinical syndromes.

Hodgkin lymphoma ★ HY

DomainDetail
EpidemiologyBimodal: age 15–35, and over 55. 50% associated with Epstein-Barr virus
DiagnosisEXCISIONAL lymph node biopsy — a needle core is usually insufficient, because the diagnosis depends on seeing the architecture around the rare malignant cells
StagingPET/CT and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. The sedimentation rate is unusual as a staging element and is worth remembering
PrognosisCurable. Better in younger adults; depends on stage, age and ESR
TreatmentABVD — doxorubicin (Adriamycin), bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine. Relapsed: stem cell transplant, brentuximab vedotin (anti-CD30 conjugate), PD-1 antibodies
🔑 The presenting features — several are peculiar to Hodgkin

Local or diffuse lymphadenopathy · pruritus · splenomegaly · B symptoms · alcohol intolerance (pain in involved nodes after drinking alcohol — rare, but essentially specific to Hodgkin) · peripheral eosinophilia · nonspecific back pain.

The combination of itching, alcohol-induced nodal pain and eosinophilia in a young adult with lymphadenopathy is a classic examination stem.

🧠 Why CD30 and PD-1 both work here

The malignant Reed-Sternberg cells express CD30, which makes them an ideal target for the antibody-drug conjugate brentuximab vedotin. Separately, Hodgkin lymphoma is unusually dependent on evading the immune cells that surround it — the tumour is mostly reactive inflammatory infiltrate — which is why PD-1 blockade is exceptionally effective in this disease compared with most cancers.

Reactive versus malignant lymphadenopathy ★ HY

FeatureReactiveMalignant
Tempo and courseFollows an identifiable trigger; regresses over weeksPersistent or progressive over weeks to months
ConsistencySoft, tender, mobileFirm, rubbery, non-tender, matted or fixed
SizeUsually under 1–2 cmLarger, and growing
Systemic featuresFever with an infective sourceB symptoms — drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss, fever
DistributionLocalized to the drainage territory of the triggerGeneralized, or supraclavicular, which is a red flag at any size
LaboratoryReactive lymphocytosis; findings of the underlying infectionRaised LDH, cytopenias, raised ESR
Definitive testEXCISIONAL biopsy with flow cytometry — architecture plus immunophenotype. A fine needle aspirate may sample only reactive cells and miss the diagnosis entirely

Q: A 68-year-old is found on routine bloods to have a lymphocyte count of 24,000. Flow cytometry shows CD5+, CD10−, CD20+, CD23+. What is the diagnosis, and does she need treatment?

Answer

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia — the immunophenotype is diagnostic. She does not need treatment on this information alone. Treatment indications are pancytopenia, bulky lymphadenopathy, severe symptoms, or threatened end organ function — a raised lymphocyte count is not among them. Risk-stratify with FISH (13q favorable; 17p or 11q high risk), IgVH status (mutated favorable) and TP53.

Q: How do you distinguish chronic lymphocytic leukemia from mantle cell lymphoma when both are CD5-positive B-cell neoplasms?

Answer

CD23. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is CD23 positive; mantle cell lymphoma is CD23 negative and carries t(11;14) with overexpression of cyclin D1. The distinction matters enormously: CLL is indolent and often needs no treatment, while mantle cell is aggressive and everyone relapses.

Q: A 24-year-old has painless cervical lymphadenopathy, itching, and reports the nodes ache after drinking beer. Bloods show eosinophilia. Likely diagnosis, and what biopsy will you request?

Answer

Hodgkin lymphoma. Alcohol intolerance, pruritus and peripheral eosinophilia together are highly characteristic, and the age fits the first peak of the bimodal 15–35 / over 55 distribution. Request an excisional lymph node biopsy, not a core needle — the diagnosis depends on nodal architecture around the rare Reed-Sternberg cells. Stage with PET/CT and an ESR. The disease is curable; treatment is ABVD.

Q: Why are aggressive lymphomas curable while indolent lymphomas generally are not?

Answer

Because chemotherapy kills dividing cells. Aggressive lymphomas have a high proliferation fraction, so cytotoxic therapy destroys nearly the whole population — hence curative intent despite death in 3–6 months untreated. Indolent lymphomas divide slowly, so most cells are never exposed to the drug's mechanism; they respond, relapse, and respond again over years.

The corollary is the tumour lysis risk: the same rapid turnover that makes aggressive disease curable makes it dangerous to treat.

Q: A patient with an IgM monoclonal protein presents with blurred vision, vertigo, ataxia and nystagmus. What is happening and what is the immediate treatment?

Answer

Hyperviscosity syndrome from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia). The immediate treatment is emergent plasmapheresis to remove the pentameric IgM. Untreated it progresses to stroke, coma and delirium. Once stabilized, treat the underlying disease — but watch for the IgM flare, a transient rise at the start of therapy.

Section 37 · Hematologic malignancy · plasma cell

Plasma Cell Disorders — Myeloma, MGUS and Smoldering Myeloma

The far right of the map: a cancer of the fully differentiated plasma cell. Its damage comes from what the cell secretes — and uniquely, it has two well-defined precursor states managed by surveillance rather than treatment.

Abbreviations used in this section MM multiple myeloma · MGUS monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance · SPEP serum protein electrophoresis — separates serum proteins to reveal a monoclonal spike · Serum light chains free immunoglobulin light chains, measured separately because they cause renal failure · Heavy chain / light chain the two protein components of an antibody · CMP comprehensive metabolic panel · Skeletal survey a series of plain radiographs looking for lytic bone lesions · Beta-2 microglobulin a serum marker of tumour burden and prognosis · Paraprotein / monoclonal protein a single antibody species produced in excess by one clone · LPL lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia) · Auto-SCT autologous stem cell transplant · PET/CT positron emission tomography with computed tomography

Workup

  • Serum protein electrophoresis — detects and quantifies the monoclonal protein
  • Serum light chains — measured separately, and the reason is below
  • Comprehensive metabolic panel — for calcium and renal function
  • Complete blood count
  • Skeletal survey; equivocal findings confirmed with PET/CT or magnetic resonance imaging
🧠 Why light chains matter so much ★ HY

Antibodies are made of a heavy chain and a light chain. A myeloma clone can produce light chains in very high concentration, and because they are small they are filtered by the glomerulus and precipitate in the tubules — causing kidney failure.

This is why serum light chains are measured separately from the electrophoresis: a patient can have significant light chain disease with an unimpressive monoclonal spike, and the kidney is the organ that pays.

🔑 The complications of plasma cell disorders — the CRAB tetrad and beyond

The end organ damage that converts a watched precursor state into a treated cancer:

  • hyperCalcemia — from bone resorption
  • Renal failure — light chain cast nephropathy, the mechanism above
  • Anemia — marrow occupation by the plasma cell clone
  • Bone lesions — lytic lesions, pathological fracture, cord compression, bone pain

Add to these: recurrent infection (the clone crowds out normal immunoglobulin production, so the patient is functionally hypogammaglobulinemic despite a high total protein), hyperviscosity, and amyloidosis from deposited light chains.

⚠️

High risk features

  • Severe anemia
  • Chronic renal failure
  • Very high monoclonal protein concentration
  • Severe hypercalcemia
  • High beta-2 microglobulin
  • FISH: 17p = bad
📆

Prognosis and treatment

Highly dependent on age, fitness, stage and FISH. Many patients will live 7–10 years or beyond.

Treatment classes: thalidomide derivatives (the “-amides”) · proteasome inhibitors · chemotherapy · monoclonal antibodies · autologous stem cell transplant · palliative radiotherapy · CAR-T · BiTE.

The precursor states — the distinction to memorize ★ HY

MGUSSmoldering myeloma
Plasma cells in marrowUnder 10%10–60%
Monoclonal proteinUnder 3 g/dL3 g/dL or more
Risk of progression1% per year — flat10% per year for the first 5 years, then 3% per year for 5 years, then 1% per year
SurveillanceSPEP, serum light chains, CBC and CMP every 6 months; skeletal survey at least annuallyThe same, except labs every 4 months, and consider an annual PET scan
TreatmentNeither is treated. Both are watched. What converts either into active myeloma is end organ damage
🔑 The two numbers that separate them: 10 and 3

10% plasma cells and 3 g/dL monoclonal protein. Below both → MGUS. Above either (up to 60% plasma cells) → smoldering.

Note the shape of the smoldering risk curve: front-loaded. A patient who gets through the first five years without progressing has a substantially lower annual risk thereafter — which is why surveillance is more intensive early.

🩺 How common is MGUS, and what to tell the patient

Most patients with MGUS will never develop myeloma — at 1% per year, an 80-year-old diagnosed with MGUS is far more likely to die of something else. The counselling point is real reassurance combined with genuine commitment to surveillance, because the 1% per year does not stop.

Myeloma versus Waldenström macroglobulinemia / lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma ★ HY

FeatureMultiple myelomaLymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström)
Cell of originFully differentiated plasma cellLymphoplasmacytic cell — a B cell with plasmacytic differentiation; an indolent lymphoma
Paraprotein classUsually IgG or IgA; light-chain-only disease occursIgM — and the pentameric structure drives every complication
GeneticsFISH abnormalities; 17p adverseMYD88 mutation
Bone lesionsLytic lesions characteristic — skeletal survey is part of the workupTypically absent
Renal failureCommon — light chain cast nephropathyUncommon
HypercalcemiaCommonUncommon
Lymphadenopathy / splenomegalyUncommonAdvanced diffuse lymphadenopathy, with or without splenomegaly
HyperviscosityUncommonCharacteristic — and an emergency needing plasmapheresis
Signature complicationsCRAB: hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, bone lesionsHyperviscosity · peripheral neuropathy · cold agglutinin hemolysis · cryoglobulinemia · bleeding from impaired fibrin polymerization
🪝 Memory hook — bone versus blood viscosity

Myeloma attacks the skeleton and the kidney. Waldenström thickens the blood and injures nerves. If the stem gives you lytic lesions, hypercalcemia and renal failure, it is myeloma. If it gives you blurred vision, vertigo, ataxia and a neuropathy in someone with lymphadenopathy, it is the IgM disease — and the treatment is plasmapheresis first, chemotherapy second.

Q: A 66-year-old has an IgG monoclonal protein of 1.8 g/dL, 6% plasma cells on marrow biopsy, normal calcium, creatinine and hemoglobin, and no bone lesions. Diagnosis, risk, and plan?

Answer

MGUS — under 10% plasma cells and under 3 g/dL monoclonal protein, with no end organ damage. Risk of progression to multiple myeloma is 1% per year. No treatment. Surveillance with SPEP, serum light chains, CBC and CMP every 6 months, plus a skeletal survey at least annually.

Q: Why can a myeloma patient develop renal failure even when the serum protein electrophoresis spike is modest?

Answer

Because of free light chains. Antibodies comprise heavy and light chains, and a clone may secrete light chains in very high concentration. Being small, they are filtered at the glomerulus and precipitate in the tubules, causing kidney failure — while contributing little to the electrophoresis peak. This is precisely why serum light chains are measured separately in the workup.

Q: How does the progression risk of smoldering myeloma differ from MGUS, and how does that change surveillance?

Answer

MGUS progresses at a flat 1% per year. Smoldering myeloma is front-loaded: 10% per year for the first 5 years, then 3% per year for 5 years, then 1% per year — roughly ten times the early risk. Accordingly surveillance is intensified: labs every 4 months rather than every 6, and consider an annual PET scan.

LO 57Source: Pharmacology of Antineoplastic Agents · Part 1

Section 38 · Antineoplastic pharmacology

Traditional Chemotherapy — Principles, Resistance and Mechanisms

The most toxic group of medications in medicine, for one reason: the thing that makes a cancer cell vulnerable is the same thing that makes your marrow, your gut lining and your hair follicles vulnerable.

Abbreviations used in this section CCS / CCNS cell cycle-specific / cell cycle-nonspecific · DHFR dihydrofolate reductase · TS thymidylate synthase · MDR1 the multi-drug resistance gene · P-glycoprotein the ATP-dependent efflux pump it encodes; the P stands for “permeability” · ATP adenosine triphosphate · 5-FU 5-fluorouracil · 6-MP / 6-TG mercaptopurine / thioguanine · HGPRT hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase · Mesna mercaptoethanesulfonate · Log kill reduction in tumour burden expressed in orders of magnitude · Narrow therapeutic index a small gap between an effective and a toxic dose
🔑 The four classes, one frame

Every antineoplastic drug belongs to exactly one of four columns, and the column tells you most of what you need to predict about it:

  • Traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy — poisons that hit any dividing cell. Toxicity = the toxicity of every fast-dividing normal tissue you own.
  • Targeted therapy — aimed at one molecule the tumour depends on. Toxicity follows the target, not the mitotic rate.
  • Immunotherapy — makes the patient's own immune system do the killing. Toxicity is autoimmunity, cytokine storm and neurotoxicity.
  • Hormonal therapy — starves a hormone-dependent tumour. Toxicity is the toxicity of hormone withdrawal.

If you can predict the adverse effect from the class before you memorize the drug, you have understood the block.

When the drug is given defines the word

Primary chemotherapy

chemotherapy alone

Used for advanced disease, or when no alternative exists. No surgery or radiation is doing part of the work.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy

given BEFORE surgery

Goal: reduce tumour size prior to resection — turn an unresectable or morbid operation into a smaller one.

Adjuvant chemotherapy

given AFTER surgery or radiation

Goal: decrease recurrence risk by treating occult micrometastases that imaging cannot see.

🪝 Memory hook — “neo-” means before

The prefix is the whole mnemonic. Neoadjuvant comes before the local therapy; plain adjuvant comes after it. Both are add-ons to a local treatment — that is what “adjuvant” means. Primary chemotherapy has no local treatment to be adjuvant to.

Basic chemotherapeutic principles that enhance efficacy ★ HY

🔑 Why almost nobody gets one drug
  • Larger spectrum of activity — a heterogeneous tumour contains subclones with different vulnerabilities; more mechanisms hit more of them.
  • Use drugs with differing mechanisms of action AND differing adverse drug reactions. Different mechanism means additive kill; different toxicity means you can give each at full dose.
  • If two drugs share the same adverse reaction, you may have to dose-reduce — the practical cost of overlapping toxicity, and exactly why the “different organ toxicity” rule exists.
  • Decrease the rate of resistance development — a cell must acquire several independent resistance mechanisms at once rather than one.

The worked example, R-CHOP — each letter is a different mechanism and a different toxicity: Rituximab (anti-CD20 antibody) · Cyclophosphamide (alkylator) · Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin (anthracycline) · Oncovin/vincristine (vinca alkaloid) · Prednisone (corticosteroid).

🧠 The log-kill hypothesis — why chemotherapy must be repeated

Cytotoxic agents follow first-order kinetics: a constant FRACTION of cells is killed by each dose, not a constant absolute number. A drug that takes the burden from 10⁸ to 10⁵ has produced a “3-log kill”.

The consequence: no single dose can ever sterilize a tumour, because a fixed fraction of any remaining population always survives. Repeated cycles are mathematically necessary, not just conventional.

The 1-gram threshold: 10⁹ cells is the smallest physically detectable burden — about 1 gram, the size of a small grape — and roughly where symptoms first appear. Everything below that line is subclinical disease you are treating blind, which is the entire justification for adjuvant chemotherapy.

Rescue therapy — giving an antidote on purpose

Rescue agentRescues fromHow it works
Leucovorin (folinic acid)MethotrexateSupplies reduced folate downstream of the blocked dihydrofolate reductase, bypassing the block in normal cells
MesnaCyclophosphamide and ifosfamideBinds the urotoxic metabolite acrolein in the bladder, preventing haemorrhagic cystitis
DexrazoxaneAnthracyclinesChelates intracellular iron so it cannot react with superoxide and hydrogen peroxide to generate free radicals — protecting cardiac muscle
⚠️ Leucovorin cuts both ways

Leucovorin is a rescue agent for methotrexate but an ENHANCER for 5-fluorouracil. Same molecule, opposite intent. Do not assume “leucovorin = antidote”.

Mechanisms of drug resistance ★ HY

Three definitions first: primary (inherent) resistance is present without prior exposure — the tumour never responded. Acquired resistance develops after exposure — the tumour responded, then stopped. Cross-resistance is resistance to one agent conferring resistance to others, including structurally unrelated ones.

MechanismWhat the cell doesDrugs affected
Increased DNA repairRepairs adducts and cross-links faster than they accumulateAlkylating agents and cisplatin
Formation of trapping agentsProduces thiol-rich molecules that bind and sequester the drug before it reaches DNABleomycin, cisplatin, anthracyclines
Changes in target enzymesAlters or amplifies the enzyme so the drug no longer inhibits itMethotrexate (dihydrofolate reductase)
Decreased activation of prodrugsLoses the activating enzyme, so the prodrug is never convertedPurine and pyrimidine antimetabolites (mercaptopurine, thioguanine, cytarabine, fluorouracil)
Drug inactivationMetabolizes the active drug to an inactive formPurine and pyrimidine antimetabolites
Decreased drug accumulationEfflux of the drug out of the cellMany anticancer drugs
Pharmacologic sanctuaryThe tumour sits where the drug cannot reachClassically the central nervous system behind the blood–brain barrier, or the testes
🧠 Multi-drug resistance and the P-glycoprotein pump

Multi-drug resistance arises from increased expression of a normal gene, MDR1, encoding the cell-surface P-glycoprotein — an ATP-dependent pump that exports drugs out of the cell. The P stands for “permeability”.

Because the pump recognizes a broad range of hydrophobic substrates, cross-resistance occurs with structurally unrelated drugs — vincristine, vinblastine, doxorubicin, bleomycin and etoposide all leave through the same door.

The same transporter is why so many anticoagulant interactions are described as “P-glycoprotein inhibitors and inducers” — verapamil, amiodarone, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, rifampicin (Section 14). One transporter, one job, many organs.

Cell cycle specificity ★ HY

🔑 The G0 problem is the whole reason cure is hard

Cells in G0 — the resting phase — are less susceptible to cancer therapy. Cell cycle-specific (CCS) drugs can only kill a cell that is currently cycling, so a tumour with a large G0 fraction is intrinsically less responsive — and slow-growing solid tumours have exactly that profile.

Cell cycle-nonspecific (CCNS) agents — alkylators, platinums, anthracyclines — do not have this limitation, which is why they remain the backbone of many regimens.

PhaseClassDrugsMechanism
G1EnzymePegaspargase, L-asparaginaseDeaminates asparagine, which leukemic cells cannot make → inhibits protein synthesis
SFolate antagonistsMethotrexate, pemetrexed, pralatrexateInhibit dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthase
SPyrimidine antagonists5-fluorouracil, capecitabine, cytarabine, gemcitabine5-FU → 5-FdUMP → inhibits thymidylate synthase → “thymidine-less death”
SPurine antagonistsMercaptopurine, thioguanine, azathioprine, fludarabineActivated by HGPRT → inhibit purine metabolism enzymes
S/G2Topoisomerase I — camptothecinsIrinotecan, topotecanStabilize the cleavable complex → single-strand breaks
Late S / early G2Topoisomerase II — podophyllotoxinsEtoposide, teniposidePersistent cleavable complex → double-strand breaks
G2Antitumour antibioticBleomycinBleomycin–iron complex → free oxygen radicals → strand breaks
MTaxanesPaclitaxel, docetaxel, cabazitaxel, nab-paclitaxelPROMOTE microtubule formation → prevent disassembly → frozen in metaphase
MVinca alkaloidsVincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbineBLOCK assembly of tubulin dimers → the spindle dissolves
CCNSAnthracyclinesDoxorubicin, daunorubicin, idarubicin, epirubicin, mitoxantroneIntercalation + topoisomerase II inhibition + free radicals
CCNSAlkylating agentsNitrogen mustards, nitrosoureas, triazenesAlkylate the nucleotide backbone of DNA
CCNSPlatinumsCisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatinIntra-strand DNA adducts, cross-linking DNA to DNA or to protein
☐ Fatal route error — vincristine is NEVER given intrathecally

Intrathecal vincristine is uniformly fatal — it causes an ascending myeloencephalopathy. This is a named, tested, absolute rule, and it is why vincristine is dispensed in a minibag rather than a syringe in most institutions.

🪝 Memory hook — stabilizer versus destabilizer

Both taxanes and vincas act on microtubules in M phase, and their effect on tubulin is opposite. Paclitaxel promotes microtubule formation and prevents disassembly — the cell is frozen in metaphase. Vincristine blocks assembly of tubulin dimers — the spindle dissolves. Both end in mitotic arrest. (Ixabepilone behaves like the taxanes; eribulin like the vincas, with less neuropathy.)

Alkylating agents and platinums — the sub-class differences

Sub-classDrugsDistinguishing toxicity
Nitrogen mustardsBendamustine, chlorambucil, mechlorethamine, melphalan, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamideHigh-dose cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide → haemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein; prevent with mesna
NitrosoureasCarmustine, lomustineNausea/vomiting and delayed myelosuppression; cross the blood–brain barrier
TriazenesDacarbazine, procarbazine, temozolomideProcarbazine is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor — carries all the tyramine interaction risk that implies
⚠️ The alkylator class signature

Myelosuppression + mucositis · neurotoxicity · SECONDARY MALIGNANCIES. The secondary-malignancy risk is the alkylators' signature — they are mutagens, which is the mechanism behind therapy-related leukemia.

FeatureCisplatinCarboplatinOxaliplatin
EmetogenicityHighly emetogenic↓—
KidneyNephrotoxicity↓—
EarOtotoxicity↓—
NervePeripheral neuropathy↓Pharyngolaryngeal dysesthesia and COLD-INDUCED neuropathy
Marrow—↑ Myelosuppression—
Shared by all three: delayed hypersensitivity reaction · metallic taste with infusion · taste changes
🔑 The platinum trade-off, in one line

Carboplatin trades cisplatin's organ toxicity for marrow toxicity. Everything cisplatin does to the kidney, the ear, the nerve and the vomiting centre, carboplatin does less of — and it pays for that with more myelosuppression. Oxaliplatin is the odd one out: its signature is cold-induced neuropathy, which patients describe as choking on cold air or cold drinks.

Q: A tumour treated with doxorubicin initially responds, then progresses. On re-challenge it is also resistant to vincristine and etoposide — drugs it has never seen and which are structurally unrelated. What is the mechanism?

Answer

Multi-drug resistance from increased expression of MDR1, producing P-glycoprotein. This is acquired resistance (it developed after exposure) that is also cross-resistance — the ATP-dependent efflux pump exports a broad range of structurally unrelated hydrophobic drugs, so resistance to one selects for resistance to all of its substrates.

Q: Why is a slowly growing solid tumour with a large G0 fraction relatively resistant to methotrexate but not to cyclophosphamide?

Answer

Methotrexate is cell cycle-specific (S phase) — it can only kill a cell actively synthesising DNA, and cells in G0 are less susceptible. Cyclophosphamide is cell cycle-nonspecific — it alkylates the DNA backbone regardless of phase, so a resting cell is still damaged and dies when it next attempts to divide.

Q: A patient on high-dose cyclophosphamide develops haematuria. Mechanism, and what should have been co-administered?

Answer

Haemorrhagic cystitis, caused by the urotoxic metabolite acrolein concentrating in the bladder. It should have been prevented with mesna, which binds acrolein in the urine, plus hydration. The same toxicity and the same prevention apply to ifosfamide.

Q: Two weeks after starting a platinum regimen, a patient reports that drinking cold water makes their throat feel like it is closing. Which platinum, and is this an allergic reaction?

Answer

Oxaliplatin. This is pharyngolaryngeal dysesthesia and cold-induced neuropathy — a neurotoxic, not an allergic, phenomenon, and specific to oxaliplatin among the three platinums. Patients are counselled to avoid cold food, drinks and air. (A separate delayed hypersensitivity reaction is shared by all three platinums, but does not present this way.)
