🩺 How to add a lecture to this file

The structure is deliberately uniform, so a new set of notes drops in without redesign:

  1. Add a section with an id matching the pattern (s45-...), and add its entry both to the sidebar navigation and to the SECTION_IDS array in the script at the bottom of the file.
  2. Tag it with the objective numbers it covers, using the same lo-badge chips, plus a lo-badge src chip naming the source notes. The badges become hover tooltips automatically — the script derives them from the badge text at load.
  3. Update the coverage map — change those rows' data-st to full, update the matching cov-status chip, and add the → §N anchor link. For a partial, set data-st="part" and give the row a data-cov attribute listing the pipe-separated phrases that are covered — the tooltip highlights those and dims the rest.
  4. Move the objective out of this section, and add any new cross-cutting facts to the Master High-Yield Checklist and the one-pager.
Every abbreviation used above, expanded

Reference

Glossary and Abbreviations

If a short form appears anywhere in this file, its long form is here — nine groups now, with the laboratory, white cell and hemostasis terms added from the Week 11 lectures. Each section also carries its own abbreviation strip at the top.

Cells, counts and morphology

CBC — complete blood count
The standard automated panel: hemoglobin, hematocrit, red cell indices, white cell count with differential, and platelet count.
Hgb — hemoglobin
The oxygen-carrying protein, measured by spectrophotometry in grams per decilitre (g/dL). Four subunits, two alpha and two beta, each carrying one oxygen molecule.
Hct — hematocrit
The percentage of whole blood volume that is red cells, measured by centrifugation. Also called packed cell volume. Roughly three times the hemoglobin.
MCV — mean corpuscular volume
Average red cell size in femtolitres (fL). Under 80 microcytic, 80–100 normocytic, over 100 macrocytic.
MCH — mean corpuscular hemoglobin
Average hemoglobin mass per red cell, in picograms. Underlies normochromic and hypochromic.
MCHC
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin per unit red cell volume. Characteristically high in hereditary spherocytosis.
RDW
Red cell distribution width — variability in cell size. Raised when two red cell populations coexist.
LDH — lactate dehydrogenase
An intracellular enzyme released when cells are destroyed. Elevated in hemolysis and in ineffective erythropoiesis.
Reticulocyte
A newly released, immature red cell still containing residual RNA. The count tells you whether the marrow is responding.
Spherocyte
A round, dense red cell with no central pallor. Hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Bite cell / blister cell
A red cell with a semicircular defect where a splenic macrophage removed a Heinz body plus membrane. G6PD deficiency.
Heinz body
An intracellular inclusion of precipitated, oxidized hemoglobin. Requires a supravital stain (crystal violet).
Target cell (codocyte)
A bull's-eye red cell, from too much membrane relative to hemoglobin content. Thalassemia, sickle cell disease, liver disease, iron deficiency.
Schistocyte
An angular red cell fragment, from mechanical shearing.
Howell-Jolly body
A retained nuclear DNA fragment in a mature red cell. Its presence means the spleen is absent or non-functional.
Macro-ovalocyte
A large, oval red cell — characteristic of megaloblastic anemia.
Hypersegmented neutrophil
A neutrophil with six or more nuclear lobes. Near-diagnostic of B12 or folate deficiency.
Anisocytosis / poikilocytosis
Variation in red cell size / variation in red cell shape. Both together is anisopoikilocytosis.
Cellularity
The proportion of marrow occupied by hematopoietic cells rather than fat: normocellular, hypercellular, hypocellular. A core-biopsy word.

Iron, vitamins and the erythron

Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺
Ferrous / ferric iron. Only the ferrous form is absorbed from the gut.
Transferrin
The plasma protein that transports iron. Picture it carrying cups that may be full or empty.
TIBC — total iron binding capacity
A measure of transferrin binding sites not saturated with iron. Rises in iron deficiency, falls in inflammation.
TSAT — transferrin saturation
The percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron. Under 15% suggests iron deficiency.
Ferritin
The intracellular iron storage protein; the serum level reflects total body stores. Also an acute phase reactant, so it rises in inflammation regardless of stores.
Hepcidin
The liver hormone, driven up by interleukin-6, that degrades ferroportin and blocks iron export from cells.
Ferroportin
The only cellular iron export channel — the door hepcidin locks.
Prussian blue stain
A histochemical stain for marrow iron. Blue granules present means stores exist; absence is diagnostic of iron deficiency.
Pica / pagophagia
Craving non-nutritive substances / craving ice specifically. Strongly associated with iron deficiency.
FOBT — fecal occult blood test
Detects blood in stool not visible to the eye.
B12 — cobalamin
Vitamin B12. Obtained from animal products. Two jobs: DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance.
IF — intrinsic factor
Secreted by gastric parietal cells; B12 must bind it to be absorbed in the terminal ileum.
MMA — methylmalonic acid
Accumulates in B12 deficiency and stays normal in folate deficiency. The key discriminator.
Homocysteine
Elevated in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot separate them.
THF — tetrahydrofolate
The active form of folate, required for thymidine and therefore DNA synthesis.
DHFR — dihydrofolate reductase
The enzyme that activates folic acid — and the enzyme methotrexate blocks.
Pernicious anemia
Autoimmune destruction of gastric mucosa causing loss of parietal cells and intrinsic factor.
Subacute combined degeneration
Degeneration of the dorsal and lateral spinal columns from B12 deficiency. Eventually irreversible.
EPO — erythropoietin
The kidney hormone that stimulates red cell production. Available as a drug (epoetin, darbepoetin).
ESA — erythropoiesis-stimulating agent
The drug class supplying that signal.
HIF-PHI
Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor — vadadustat. Oral; convinces the cell it is at altitude.
Ineffective erythropoiesis
Precursors produced but destroyed within the marrow before release — hypercellular marrow with a low reticulocyte count.
NTD — neural tube defect
Spina bifida and anencephaly; prevented by pre-conception folic acid.

Hemolysis and hemoglobinopathies

Haptoglobin
The plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin after intravascular hemolysis. Consumed in the process, so serum levels fall.
Hemopexin
A second scavenger, which binds free heme rather than intact hemoglobin.
Hemoglobinemia / hemoglobinuria
Free hemoglobin in plasma (pink plasma) / in urine (dark, tea-coloured).
RES — reticuloendothelial system
The macrophage network of spleen, liver and marrow that clears damaged cells and hemoglobin complexes.
DAT — direct antiglobulin test
The direct Coombs test. Detects antibody already coating the patient's own red cells.
Osmotic fragility test
Red cells in hypotonic saline. Spherocytes have no spare membrane and lyse where normal cells do not.
G6PD
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase — the red cell's only meaningful source of NADPH.
NADPH
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate, reduced form. Powers glutathione reductase.
HbA / HbF / HbA₂
Adult hemoglobin α₂β₂ / fetal hemoglobin α₂γ₂ / α₂δ₂, raised in beta thalassemia.
HbS
Sickle hemoglobin — valine for glutamic acid at the 6th codon of beta globin.
HbH / Hb Barts
β₄ (one alpha gene remaining) / γ₄ (no alpha genes; hydrops fetalis). Both are unpartnered-chain tetramers.
HPLC
High performance liquid chromatography — separates hemoglobins for identification; now more common than gel electrophoresis.
BCL11A
The gene that switches fetal hemoglobin off after birth; the target of Casgevy.
Autosplenectomy
Destruction of the spleen by repeated infarction, as in sickle cell disease. Produces functional asplenia.
PNH
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria — deficiency of the complement regulators CD55 and CD59, causing intravascular hemolysis and a prothrombotic state.

Transfusion medicine

FFP — fresh frozen plasma
The plasma fraction, frozen. Contains all coagulation, fibrinolytic and complement proteins.
Cryoprecipitate
The cold-insoluble precipitate formed when frozen plasma is thawed at refrigerated temperature. Rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII.
Apheresis
Drawing blood from a donor, separating one component in line, and returning the rest.
Citrate
The anticoagulant in every blood bag. Chelates calcium. A large load during massive transfusion causes hypocalcemia.
Leukocyte reduction
Filtering white cells out of a product. Reduces febrile reactions and HLA alloimmunization.
Irradiation
Damaging the DNA of residual donor lymphocytes so they cannot proliferate. The only prevention for transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
PCC — prothrombin complex concentrate
A concentrated plasma-derived product containing vitamin K-dependent factors. 3-factor and 4-factor forms. Preferred over plasma for urgent warfarin reversal.
IVIG
Intravenous immunoglobulin — pooled, purified human antibody, dispensed from pharmacy.
MTP — massive transfusion protocol
A single activation sending a standard box of all products to the bedside.
ABO / RhD
The major blood group systems. RhD positive means the D antigen is present; about 15% of people are D negative.
HLA — human leukocyte antigen
The tissue type system. Anti-HLA antibodies from parous donors cause TRALI.
Alloimmunization
Forming an antibody against a foreign red cell antigen. Only two routes of exposure: transfusion and pregnancy.
Type and screen / type and cross
Screen = ready (type + antibody screen, no units held). Cross = reserved (units crossmatched and held for that patient).
TRALI
Transfusion-related acute lung injury. Hypotensive, normal JVP, donor anti-HLA antibodies, within 6 hours.
TACO
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload. Hypertensive, raised JVP, responds to diuresis.
GVHD
Graft-versus-host disease. Transfusion-associated form presents 1–6 weeks later with pancytopenia; prevented only by irradiation.
WBIT — wrong blood in tube
The labelling error that causes fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion.
DIC
Disseminated intravascular coagulation — simultaneous widespread clotting and clot breakdown; consumes fibrinogen.

Hemostasis pharmacology

UFH / LMWH
Unfractionated / low-molecular-weight heparin. Both act through antithrombin; chain length determines which factors are reached.
aPTT / PT / INR
Activated partial thromboplastin time (monitors heparin) / prothrombin time / international normalized ratio (monitors warfarin).
HIT
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Antibodies to the heparin–platelet factor 4 complex activate platelets; the danger is thrombosis.
PF4
Platelet factor 4 — the protein heparin binds to form the antigenic complex in HIT.
DOAC
Direct oral anticoagulant — dabigatran and the “-xabans”.
VKORC1
Vitamin K epoxide reductase complex 1 — warfarin's target; genetic variants alter dose requirement.
CYP2C9 / CYP3A4 / CYP2C19
Cytochrome P450 enzymes. 2C9 metabolizes warfarin; 3A4 governs the -xabans and the HIV boosters; 2C19 activates clopidogrel.
P-gp
P-glycoprotein — a drug-transport pump; all three -xabans are substrates.
CrCl
Creatinine clearance — a measure of kidney function used to dose-adjust anticoagulants.
COX / TXA₂
Cyclooxygenase / thromboxane A2 — aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, abolishing thromboxane for the platelet's lifespan.
P2Y12
The platelet ADP receptor blocked by clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor and cangrelor.
GP IIb/IIIa
Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa — the fibrinogen receptor and the final common step of platelet aggregation.
PAR-1
Protease-activated receptor 1 — the thrombin receptor on the platelet, blocked by vorapaxar.
PDE / cAMP
Phosphodiesterase / cyclic adenosine monophosphate — dipyridamole and cilostazol raise cAMP to keep platelets calm.
tPA
Tissue plasminogen activator — alteplase. Converts plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin.
TXA
Tranexamic acid — an antifibrinolytic, the mirror image of the “-plase” drugs.
TFPI
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor — a natural anticoagulant blocked by marstacimab and concizumab in hemophilia.
G-CSF / GM-CSF
Granulocyte, and granulocyte-macrophage, colony-stimulating factor. Given as filgrastim and sargramostim.

Sepsis and HIV

SIRS
Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome. No longer defining for sepsis but still used by the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
SOFA / qSOFA
Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (score ≥ 2 ≈ 10% mortality) / quick SOFA (respiratory rate ≥ 22, systolic pressure ≤ 100, altered mentation).
NEWS2 / MEWS
National Early Warning Score, 6 parameters including oxygen saturation / Modified Early Warning Score, 5 parameters, more sensitive.
MODS
Multi-Organ Dysfunction Syndrome — the older term for the end state of septic shock.
PAMPs / DAMPs
Pathogen-Associated / Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns. Viral sepsis works through DAMPs, not PAMPs.
LPS
Lipopolysaccharide — the most prominent gram-negative trigger.
Procalcitonin
The one sepsis marker that points to a cause — elevation indicates a bacterial etiology.
PSS
Post-sepsis syndrome, affecting 50% of survivors.
ART
Antiretroviral therapy. Called HAART in the 1990s.
NRTI / NNRTI / INSTI / PI
Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (competitive, chain-terminating) / non-nucleoside (allosteric) / integrase strand transfer inhibitor / protease inhibitor.
gp120 / gp41
The env products — the binding protein and the fusion protein.
p24
The gag capsid antigen; easiest HIV protein to detect in serum, and the basis of 4th-generation testing.
PIC / RTC
Pre-integration complex / reverse transcription complex — chaperoned into the nucleus by capsid material.
NAT
Nucleic acid test (HIV-1 RNA PCR) — the third tier of the CDC algorithm; a positive result there means acute infection.
ARS
Acute retroviral syndrome — primary HIV infection. Non-exudative pharyngitis is the discriminator from strep.
IRIS
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome — paradoxical or unmasking; median 48 days after starting ART.
PJP
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Cholesterol not ergosterol in the cell wall, which is why TMP/SMX and not an azole.
TMP/SMX
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole — treatment and prophylaxis for PJP, and prophylaxis for toxoplasmosis.
TDF / TAF
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (more nephrotoxic, more bone loss) / tenofovir alafenamide (less).
PrEP / PEP
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (~99% effective for sexual transmission) / post-exposure prophylaxis (start within 72 hours, take for a month).
U = U
Undetectable equals untransmittable — CDC threshold < 200 copies/mL. Evidence: the PARTNER trial.

The laboratory — methods and artefacts

Coulter principle (impedance)
A cell crossing a narrow aperture changes electrical impedance. Each pulse is one cell; pulse height is proportional to size. Gives RBC + MCV, platelets + MPV, and the total white count.
Flow cytometry
Separates cells by forward scatter (size) against side scatter (complexity and granularity). The basis of the automated white cell differential, and of the scattergram flags.
SLS — sodium lauryl sulfate
The cyanide-free hemoglobin reagent. Lyses cells, oxidises heme, and forms a stable coloured complex read photometrically at 555 nm.
PLT-F
The fluorescent platelet channel. Stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with oxazine, counting by content rather than size. Correlates with CD41/CD61; used below 50 × 10³/µL.
RDW — red cell distribution width
The width of the impedance size distribution, calculated as SD of volume / MCV. Normal 11.4–14.5. Raised with a normal MCV means two populations.
Immature platelet fraction
Newly released platelets — the platelet equivalent of the reticulocyte count. Used to detect marrow recovery after transplant days before the count rises.
Accuracy vs precision
Systematic bias reduces accuracy (suspect the instrument, recalibrate); random bias reduces precision (may be intrinsic to the assay). Platelets vary 15–20% intrinsically; the MCV is very tight.
Autoverification
Automatic release of results when there are no flags and values are near normal, without human review.
Ghost cells
Cells that lysed during collection or processing. Low forward and side scatter, gated out as debris; a lot of them means a degraded sample.
Monolayer / feather edge
The monolayer is where cells sit evenly spaced without overlapping — the only region morphology should be read in. The feather edge distorts cells and manufactures spherocytes.
Wright–Giemsa stain
Eosin plus methylene blue, devised in 1902. Hematoxylin is a basic dye staining acidic DNA blue; eosin is an acidic dye staining basic cytoplasmic protein pink.
Cold agglutinin
An antibody clumping red cells at low temperature. Clumps count as one large cell → low RBC, high MCV, and an impossibly high MCHC. Resolved by warming the sample to 37 °C.
Pseudothrombocytopenia
A falsely low platelet count from EDTA-dependent clumping. Confirmed on the smear; resolved by redrawing into citrate.
Codocyte / dacryocyte / acanthocyte / echinocyte
Target cell (excess membrane for the contents) / tear-drop cell (myelofibrosis) / spur cell, few irregular spicules (liver) / burr cell, many even spicules (uremia, or a drying artefact).
Polychromasia
Larger blue-grey red cells on the smear — reticulocytes. The morphological equivalent of a raised reticulocyte count.
Parasitaemia
The percentage of red cells infected in malaria. Reported with every smear; drives treatment intensity and monitors response.

White cells and immunodeficiency

ANC — absolute neutrophil count
White cell count × % neutrophils — an absolute number, never a percentage. Under 1,000 infection risk climbs; under 500 endogenous flora escape control; under 200 no inflammatory response is possible.
Left shift
Circulating immature granulocyte precursors — bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes — because the marrow is releasing cells early under demand.
Auer rod
A needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusion in a myeloblast. A marker of malignancy, specifically a myeloid leukemia.
Döhle body / toxic granulation / vacuolisation
The three reactive neutrophil changes — retained rough endoplasmic reticulum, coarse dark granules, and phagocytic vacuoles. Signs of a cell working hard, not a malignant clone.
Leukemoid reaction
Severe leukocytosis with immature cells in the blood that may mimic a neoplastic proliferation. Differential: myelofibrosis and a space-occupying marrow lesion.
Leukoerythroblastic picture
Immature white cells plus nucleated red cells plus tear-drop cells together — disturbed marrow architecture.
N:C ratio / clonality
Nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio: decreased favours reactive, increased favours malignant. A monoclonal, uniform population favours malignancy; a variety of appearances favours a reactive process.
B symptoms
Fever, night sweats, weight loss — systemic features raising concern for lymphoma or leukemia.
Duffy null
A common variant, particularly in people of African ancestry, giving a constitutionally lower neutrophil count with no increased infection risk. The same antigen is Plasmodium vivax's red cell receptor.
CGD — chronic granulomatous disease
NADPH oxidase / cytochrome b558 mutations; phagocytes cannot generate reactive oxygen species, so catalase-positive organisms survive inside them. Diagnosed by nitroblue tetrazolium or the neutrophil oxidative index.
Catalase-positive
An organism that destroys its own hydrogen peroxide, leaving a CGD phagocyte nothing to borrow: S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia, Burkholderia.
BTK — Bruton tyrosine kinase
Mutated in X-linked agammaglobulinemia; the block sits at the pre-B cell, so there are no CD19/CD20 B cells, no plasma cells and no tonsils.
CATCH-22
DiGeorge syndrome: Cardiac abnormality, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, chromosome 22q11 — one third/fourth branchial pouch migration defect.
SCID / TREC
Severe combined immunodeficiency; screened for at birth by T-cell receptor excision circles, a by-product of normal T-cell receptor rearrangement. An absolute lymphocyte count below 2,000/µL warrants evaluation.
ADA — adenosine deaminase
The autosomal recessive SCID enzyme. Accumulated purines inhibit ribonucleotide reductase; because the defect is systemic, neurological problems can persist after a successful transplant.

Bleeding and clotting

PT / INR / aPTT
Prothrombin time (extrinsic + common, most sensitive to factor 7) / its standardised form, the number warfarin is dosed against / activated partial thromboplastin time (intrinsic + common, most sensitive to factors 8, 9, 11, 12).
Mixing study
Patient plasma mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma. Corrects → factor deficiency. Fails to correct → inhibitor. Incubate 30–60 min at 37 °C to catch a slow factor 8 antibody.
The 50% rule
Roughly 50% of a factor is enough for hemostasis — which is why clotting times only prolong well below normal, and why adding an equal volume of normal plasma corrects a deficiency.
D-dimer
A fragment carrying two D regions, released only when factor 13-cross-linked fibrin is degraded by plasmin. A marker of clot turnover, not merely of clotting.
Sodium citrate tube
The light-blue-top coagulation tube. Citrate binds calcium reversibly so the laboratory can restart clotting; the 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio must be exact or times are falsely prolonged.
VWF:Ag / VWF:RCo
Von Willebrand factor antigen (how much protein) versus ristocetin cofactor activity (how well it works). A ratio under about 0.5–0.7 means a qualitative, type 2 defect.
Ristocetin
A withdrawn antibiotic that forces von Willebrand factor onto platelet GPIb. Its side effect became the assay's mechanism.
HMWM / ADAMTS13
High molecular weight multimers carry most of von Willebrand factor's activity; ADAMTS13 is the protease that trims them. Losing the large ones causes bleeding; failing to trim them causes TTP.
GPIb/IX/V vs GPIIb/IIIa
The von Willebrand factor receptor (absent in Bernard–Soulier — low ristocetin, large platelets) versus the fibrinogen receptor, CD41/CD61 (absent in Glanzmann — everything but ristocetin low).
Emicizumab (Hemlibra)
A bispecific antibody bridging factor 9a and factor 10, reproducing factor 8a's cofactor geometry. Works despite an anti-factor-8 inhibitor, and falsely shortens the aPTT.
DDAVP — desmopressin
Releases stored von Willebrand factor and factor 8 from endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies. First-line in type 1 von Willebrand disease; potentially harmful in type 2B.
TMA — thrombotic microangiopathy
Small-vessel thrombosis with mechanical red cell destruction. TTP, HUS and aHUS all have normal PT, aPTT and fibrinogen — which is what separates them from DIC.
Eculizumab
An anti-C5 monoclonal antibody; the targeted therapy for atypical HUS, where the alternative complement pathway runs unregulated.
Virchow's triad
Endothelial cell damage, blood stasis, and a hypercoagulable state — the three categories of thrombosis risk.
Factor V Leiden / activated protein C resistance
The R506Q mutation that prevents protein C from cleaving factor 5a. The commonest thrombophilia (~5% of Caucasians, 20–30% of VTE) and one of the least dangerous (RR 3–5×).
Prothrombin G20210A
A 3′ untranslated region mutation raising pre-messenger-RNA stability, so more prothrombin is made. The protein is normal — hence molecular, not functional, testing.
Purpura fulminans
Neonatal dermal microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis in homozygous protein C or S deficiency. The purpura is a consequence of the clotting, not of bleeding.
Lupus anticoagulant
A double misnomer: patients need not have lupus, and it prolongs clotting in vitro while promoting thrombosis in vivo. Fails to correct on mixing but corrects with added phospholipid.
dRVVT
Dilute Russell viper venom test — a phospholipid-dependent clotting assay, more specific than the aPTT for a lupus anticoagulant.
HIT / PF4 / 4T score / SRA
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — antibody against the heparin–platelet factor 4 complex, days 5–14, prothrombotic despite the low count. The 4T score (Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher cause) decides whether to test; the serotonin release assay resolves a conflicting immunoassay.
Anti-Xa
Anti-factor 10a activity. The only valid assay for low-molecular-weight heparin and fondaparinux, because only a long heparin chain bridges antithrombin to thrombin for the aPTT to sense.
Argatroban / lepirudin
Direct thrombin inhibitors used in HIT, where no heparin compound and no warfarin alone may be given.
OMK 2A Hematology · Summative 3 · Objective Review · UNE COM — for personal study use only Keys: J/K sections · Q next question · R reveal · H one-pager · Esc close

🎯 Hematology Summative 3 — High-Yield One-Pager

Condensed by objective cluster — hematopoiesis · anemia I & II · the laboratory · benign white cells · bleeding · clotting · transfusion · pharmacology · sepsis · HIV · malignancy · antineoplastics · lymphatics · VTE. Covers the 83 fully-covered and 6 partially-covered study guide objectives.

Hematopoiesis · LO 1 · 88 · 93 · 94

Sites & hierarchy

  • Yolk sac → fetal liver & spleen → bone marrow. Adult: vertebrae, ribs, sternum, pelvis (axial).
  • HSC = self-renewal + differentiation; multipotent. Over-self-renewal = leukemia.
  • Myeloid: RBC, megakaryocyte→platelet, neutrophil, mono→macrophage, eos, baso. Lymphoid: T (thymus), B (marrow)→plasma cell, NK.
  • Platelet = anucleate membrane fragment → aspirin lasts its 7–10 day life.
  • Extramedullary hematopoiesis + skull/face marrow expansion → frontal bossing in thalassemia.

Hormones → drugs

  • EPO (kidney) → RBC · TPO → platelets · G-CSF/GM-CSF → granulocytes · GH/IGF → lymphocytes.
  • Retic low = production problem. Retic high = loss/destruction.

Marrow biopsy & CBC

  • Prone, posterior superior iliac spine. Aspirate = cytology; core = architecture/cellularity.
  • Hypercellular → leukemia or compensatory drive. Hypocellular → aplastic anemia, MDS, post-chemo.
  • Do NOT biopsy for routine anemia.
  • Hct ≈ 3 × Hgb. Female 37–47%, male 42–52%. RDW ↑ = two populations.
  • Acute hemorrhage: initial Hgb can be normal — concentration unchanged.
Anemia I · LO 7 · 11 · 23 · 25 · 26 · 37 · 50 · 66 · 81

The 3 buckets + the algorithm

  • Blood loss · impaired production · increased destruction.
  • Confirm → read MCV first → retic count → targeted study → smear.
  • <80 micro · 80–100 normo · >100 macro.

Iron deficiency

  • Fe ↓, ferritin ↓, TIBC ↑, TSAT <15%, MCV ↓, marrow iron absent.
  • Stations: duodenum (Fe²⁺ only) → transferrin → cells → ferritin.
  • Adult male or postmenopausal female = GI blood loss until proven otherwise → colonoscopy.
  • Ferritin is an acute phase reactant — can be falsely normal.
  • Small AND pale: extra divisions before maturation.

B12 · pernicious · folate

  • B12 = DNA synthesis + myelin. Folate = DNA only. B12 has the Brain.
  • Megaloblastic: macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (≥6 lobes), hypercellular marrow, retic low, LDH high = ineffective erythropoiesis.
  • MMA elevated in B12, normal in folate. Homocysteine ↑ in both.
  • PA = autoimmune loss of parietal cells → no IF. Anti-parietal 85–90% (sensitive), anti-IF 75% (specific). Triad: anemia + gastric atrophy (cancer risk) + subacute combined degeneration.
  • Path: pepsin → haptocorrin → pancreatic proteases → IF → terminal ileum → transcobalamin II.
  • Drug causes: metformin (ileum), PPI (stomach).
  • Never folate alone — corrects the count while the cord degenerates.
  • Folate in pregnancy: neural tube closes at ~4 weeks — supplement before conception.
The laboratory · LO 35 · 50

Measured vs calculated

  • Measured: RBC + MCV (impedance), Hgb (SLS photometry, 555 nm).
  • Calculated: Hct = RBC×MCV/10 · MCH = Hgb/RBC×10 · MCHC = Hgb/Hct×100 · RDW = SD/MCV.
  • Ranges: RBC 3.5–5.5 ×10⁶ · MCV 80–100 fL (lower in children) · MCHC 31–37 · RDW 11.4–14.5 · retics 0.8–4%.
  • Hct ≈ 3 × Hgb, only if the MCV is normal. Breaking the rule is itself a finding.
  • EDTA (lavender) ≤3 h ideal, ≤8 h acceptable. Citrate is the fallback for platelets.

Interferences

  • MCHC >37 g/dL = artefact — except hereditary spherocytosis.
  • Cold agglutinins: ↓RBC, ↑MCV, ↑↑MCHC → warm to 37 °C.
  • Microcytes/schistocytes/WBC fragments → falsely HIGH platelets. Clumps/giant platelets → falsely LOW → citrate tube or PLT-F channel.
  • Lipemia, huge WBC, bilirubin → falsely high Hgb. nRBCs → falsely high WBC.

The smear

  • Read the monolayer — the feather edge manufactures spherocytes.
  • Spherocyte → HS / autoimmune · target → thalassemia, HbC, liver, splenectomy · tear-drop → myelofibrosis · acanthocyte (few, irregular) → liver · echinocyte (many, even) → uremia/artefact · schistocyte → microangiopathy.
  • Target cells → send hemoglobin electrophoresis. Morphology cannot call thalassemia.
  • Malaria: fever + travel + thrombocytopenia. Report parasitaemia %. P. falciparum >10%, infects all ages; vivax/ovale form hypnozoites.

Anemia of inflammation

  • Most common anemia in hospitalized US patients. Ferritin ↑, TIBC ↓.
  • IL-6 → hepcidin ↑ → degrades ferroportin → iron locked in macrophages/enterocytes. Plus ↓EPO, ↓erythroid proliferation, ↑hemophagocytosis.
  • Treat the underlying disease. Oral iron does not work; IV iron bypasses the locked door.

3 microcytics, 3 treatments

FerritinTIBCDo
Iron def↓↑Give iron
Inflammation↑↓Treat disease
Thal traitnormalnormalNothing
Anemia II · LO 5 · 12 · 32 · 36 · 86 · 89

Intravascular vs extravascular

  • Shared: short lifespan · ↑ unconjugated bilirubin · compensatory retic ↑.
  • Intravascular triad: pink plasma · dark urine · absent haptoglobin. Schistocytes. Kidney at risk — free heme is nephrotoxic.
  • Extravascular: spherocytes, splenomegaly, haptoglobin only mildly low.

Match the cell

  • Ball → spherocytosis · Bite → G6PD · Bull's-eye → thalassemia · Crescent → sickle · Fragment → microangiopathic · Howell-Jolly → no spleen.

The four inherited defects

  • HS — AD, cytoskeleton (ANK1/SPTB/SLC4A1). MCHC ↑, osmotic fragility ↑, Coombs NEGATIVE. Tx: folate, transfusion, splenectomy.
  • G6PD — X-linked; enzyme unstable, so old cells fail. Bite/blister cells, Heinz bodies (supravital stain). Triggers: infection (commonest), sulfa/antimalarials/nitrofurantoin, fava beans. Assay falsely normal during a crisis — repeat at 2–3 months. A− class III (mild) vs Mediterranean class II (severe).
  • Thalassemia — 4 alpha genes (chr 16), 2 beta (chr 11). The unpaired partner is the poison. HbH = β₄ (1 alpha gene); Hb Barts = γ₄ (0 alpha) = hydrops. Beta major presents at 3–6 months when the globin switch happens. Electrophoresis: ↑HbF, ↑HbA₂. Tx: transfusion + chelation.
  • Sickle — glutamic acid → valine, 6th codon, HBB. Deoxy-HbS polymerizes. Disease = HbS 90–100%, HbA absent; trait = 40–45% HbS + HbA.

Sickle — crises & management

  • Aplastic → retic LOW (parvovirus B19). Sequestration → retic high + huge spleen. Vaso-occlusive → Hgb near baseline; dactylitis in infants.
  • Worse with ↑HbS%, ↑concentration (dehydration), acidosis.
  • Hydroxyurea ↑HbF — boxed: myelosuppression + carcinogenic. Penicillin prophylaxis + pneumococcal/meningococcal/Hib. Folic acid. Chronic transfusion to HbS < 30% for stroke prevention. Casgevy (CRISPR, BCL11A) / Lyfgenia (lentiviral beta gene), age ≥12.
  • Fever in a sickle child = emergency (autosplenectomy).

Asplenia

  • Encapsulated organisms: S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae b.
  • Prevent: vaccinate (before surgery if planned) · daily penicillin in children · any fever is an emergency.
Benign WBC · LO 4 · 42 · 59 · 77

Counts & the ANC

  • WBC 4.3–10.8 ×10⁹/L. Neutrophils 45–74% · lymphocytes 16–45% · monocytes 4–10% · eos 0–7% · baso 0–2%.
  • ANC = WBC × % neutrophils. <1,000 risk ↑ · <500 own flora · <200 no inflammatory response — fever may be the only sign.
  • Neutropenia: adults → drugs, children → infections; also destruction, sequestration, pooling.
  • Duffy null = constitutionally low ANC, no infection risk. Same antigen P. vivax uses.

Reactive vs malignant

  • Reactive: ↓N:C, cytoplasmic “skirt”, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, varied, other lines normal.
  • Malignant: ↑N:C, scant cytoplasm, open chromatin, prominent nucleoli, monoclonal, cytopenias.
  • Blast pyramid: reactive keeps normal proportions; more blasts than anything = leukemia. Auer rod = malignant; a nucleolus alone is not.
  • Leukemoid: Döhle bodies, toxic granules, vacuoles + myelocytes + nRBC + tear-drops = leukoerythroblastic → myelofibrosis or a space-occupying lesion. Basophilia → think CML (BCR-ABL).

Immunodeficiencies

  • Shares: antibody 65% · combined 15% · phagocyte 10% · cellular 5% · complement 5%.
  • CGD: NADPH oxidase/cytochrome b558, 70% X-linked; catalase-positive organisms survive → granulomas. NBT test. IFN-γ ↓infection up to 70%.
  • Bruton: BTK, X-linked, well ~6 months (maternal IgG), no CD19/CD20, absent tonsils → monthly IgG.
  • DiGeorge: 22q11, CATCH-22, 3rd/4th branchial pouch → irradiated blood products, no live vaccines.
  • SCID: common γ chain or ADA; sick from month 2; TREC newborn screen, ALC <2,000 → transplant, earlier is better.
Bleeding · LO 39 · 48 · 61 · 83

Pattern → half of hemostasis

  • Mucocutaneous → VWD / platelets (primary) · joint + muscle → hemophilia (secondary) · delayed → factor 13 or antiplasmin.
  • Intrinsic 12→11→9→8 = aPTT · extrinsic 7 = PT · common 10→5→2→fibrinogen = both. Liver makes all except VWF and factor 8.
  • 50% rule: aPTT prolongs ~50%, 30–40% still fine, <20% = hemophilia (>45 s), <1% severe (>100 s).
  • Mix corrects → deficiency; fails → inhibitor. Incubate 30–60 min at 37 °C for a slow factor 8 antibody.
  • Blind spot: PT/aPTT are plasma assays — VWD and platelet defects are invisible. Citrate tube 9:1 or falsely prolonged.

The named disorders

  • Hemophilia A = factor 8 (1:5,000 M), B = factor 9 (1:30,000 M), both X-linked; C = factor 11, autosomal, mild. Factor 12 prolongs the aPTT and does not bleed.
  • Severity <1% severe · 1–5% moderate · >5–30% mild. Treat to 20–30%. Inhibitor → emicizumab (bridges 9a–10).
  • VWD: commonest inherited bleeding disorder, autosomal dominant. Activity ≈ antigen → quantitative (1, 3); activity ≪ antigen (<0.5–0.7) → type 2. DDAVP for type 1; concentrate for 2B and 3. Group O runs lower.
  • Handshake: collagen→VWF→GPIb→platelet. Bernard–Soulier = GPIb missing (↓ristocetin, big platelets) · Glanzmann = GPIIb/IIIa (all but ristocetin ↓; aspirin looks the same).
  • Acquired: liver (rebalanced, INR misleads) · DIC (↓plt, ↑PT/aPTT, ↓fibrinogen trend, ↑↑D-dimer, schistocytes → treat the cause) · vitamin K (2,7,9,10 + C/S; factor 5 normal = vitamin K, low = liver) · acquired inhibitor (older, new diathesis, mix fails).
Transfusion · LO 20 · 38 · 54 · 71

Products & thresholds

  • RBC 1–6 °C, 42 d · Platelets room temp, agitated, 5–7 d · Plasma frozen 1 yr · Cryo = fibrinogen.
  • TRICC: transfuse < 7 g/dL, one unit then reassess. Liberal arm did worse.
  • Platelets: 10k hypoproliferative · 20k lumbar puncture · 25k preterm neonate. Not for ITP/dengue (consumptive).
  • 30% factor activity is enough to clot — ocean vs teacup. INR 1.1 needs nothing.
  • Warfarin reversal: 4F-PCC + vitamin K, not plasma.
  • Citrate chelates calcium → hypocalcemia in massive transfusion.

Immunohematology

  • ABO antibodies are naturally occurring IgM from infant gut flora → fix complement → intravascular. Alloantibodies are IgG from transfusion/pregnancy → extravascular.
  • O = universal RBC donor; AB = universal RBC recipient. Inverts for plasma.
  • 15% RhD negative; O-negative ≈ 6%. Save D-negative for females of childbearing potential.
  • Alloimmunization 1–3% general, 20–60% in sickle cell disease.
  • Direct Coombs = on the cell (diagnosis). Indirect = in the plasma (the screen).
  • Screen = ready. Cross = reserved.

Reactions

  • Steps: stop → keep line open → clerical check → treat → send to blood bank.
  • Febrile non-hemolytic (cytokines; prevent by leukoreduction) · Septic (platelets, room temp) · Acute hemolytic ABO (back/flank pain, pink plasma, DAT+, “never event”, from wrong blood in tube) · Allergic / anaphylaxis (IgA deficiency, washed products).
  • TRALI: hypotensive, normal JVP, donor anti-HLA (14–20% of parous women), <6 h, diuresis no help. TACO: hypertensive, raised JVP, diuresis helps.
  • Transfusion GVHD: pancytopenia 1–6 wk, usually fatal. Prevent by irradiation — also for related donors.
  • Most common infectious risk = bacterially contaminated platelet.
Pharmacology · LO 13 · 14 · 19 · 34 · 55 · 62 · 65 · 68 · 69 · 78

Anticoagulants

  • UFH = long rope (IIa + Xa) · LMWH = short (mostly Xa) · fondaparinux = pentasaccharide (pure Xa, no HIT, no reversal).
  • Protamine: full → partial → none.
  • HIT: platelets fall 5–10 d, >50% drop; danger is thrombosis. Stop all heparin; give argatroban/bivalirudin/fondaparinux. Never warfarin alone (protein C → limb gangrene).
  • Warfarin: VKORC1 → factors II, VII, IX, X + protein C & S (“1972”). Factor VII shortest half-life → INR moves before the patient is anticoagulated → bridge ≥5 days. Teratogenic.
  • ↑INR: amiodarone, metronidazole, TMP/SMX, fluconazole, cipro, acute alcohol binge, gut-flora-killing antibiotics. ↓INR: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort, chronic alcohol, leafy greens. Pharmacogenomics: CYP2C9 + VKORC1.
  • Xabans: Apixaban all-round safest · Rivaroxaban requires a meal · Edoxaban avoid if CrCl >95.
  • Reversal: protamine · vitamin K + 4F-PCC · idarucizumab (dabigatran) · 4F-PCC (xabans) · nothing (fondaparinux).

Antiplatelets & fibrinolytics

  • White clot (arterial) = antiplatelet. Red clot (venous) = anticoagulant.
  • Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 for the platelet's 7–10 day life; low dose is the antiplatelet dose.
  • Clopidogrel = prodrug, CYP2C19 (avoid omeprazole; use pantoprazole) · prasugrel contraindicated after stroke/TIA · ticagrelor reversible, dyspnea, aspirin ≤100 mg · cangrelor IV, minutes.
  • GP IIb/IIIa (eptifibatide, tirofiban): thrombocytopenia + worst bleeding. Vorapaxar: absolute contraindication with prior stroke/TIA/ICH. Cilostazol: boxed — contraindicated in heart failure.
  • -plase = plasminogen activator. Tenecteplase = single bolus, now approved for stroke. Catastrophic bleed → cryoprecipitate + tranexamic acid.

Anemia drugs

  • Oral iron: Fe²⁺ only, acidic duodenum; avoid enteric-coated/SR; alternate-day dosing; retic bump 7–10 d; continue 3–6 months past normalization.
  • IV iron: premedicate with methylprednisolone, NOT diphenhydramine. Ferric carboxymaltose → hypophosphatemia (FGF23) + heart failure indication.
  • Iron toxicity: acute → deferoxamine. Chronic overload → deferasirox (renal/hepatic/GI boxed), deferiprone (agranulocytosis), deferoxamine (8–12 h infusions, ocular/auditory).
  • ESAs: stimulate erythroid progenitor division/differentiation + retic release. IV or SC (SC needs 15–30% less). Approved: CKD + chemotherapy anemia. 4 boxed warnings, all at Hgb > 11 g/dL; cut the dose if it rises >1 g/dL in 2 weeks. HTN in up to ⅓. Replete iron first.
  • Leucovorin bypasses DHFR — the rescue for methotrexate. Luspatercept unblocks late maturation in thalassemia.
  • Complement inhibitors (PNH) → boxed meningococcal warning, vaccinate first.
Sepsis & HIV · LO 16 · 28 · 30 · 31 · 33 · 73 · 80

Sepsis

  • Dysregulated host response. Cultures negative in 30–50%. 1.7 M cases, ~350k deaths, $62 B/yr.
  • SOFA ≥ 2 ≈ 10% mortality. qSOFA: RR ≥22, SBP ≤100, altered mentation. NEWS2 = 6 params (adds O₂ sat); MEWS = 5, more sensitive. SIRS criteria are bidirectional.
  • Source order: respiratory > urinary > abdominal. 20% polymicrobial. Abdominal → B. fragilis.
  • G(−) → LPS · G(+) → lipoteichoic acid + peptidoglycan · fungal → β-glucans/mannans/chitin · viral → DAMPs.
  • Inflammation → endothelial dysfunction + ischemia → sequential organ failure → necrosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, autophagy.
  • Procalcitonin = the one cause-specific marker (bacterial). Bundle: bactericidal antibiotic, IV fluids, lactate, assess perfusion, vasopressors + source control.
  • Mortality 10–52%; post-sepsis syndrome in 50% of survivors; 90% survival if young/healthy.

HIV

  • pol → RT (high error rate), integrase, protease · gag → p24 (easiest to detect), p17, p6/7/9 · env → gp120 (binds CD4/CCR5/CXCR4), gp41 (fusion). gag/pol cleaved by viral protease; env by host protease.
  • Cycle → drug: attachment/fusion (fostemsavir gp120, maraviroc CCR5, enfuvirtide gp41, ibalizumab post-attachment) · RT (NRTI competitive/chain-terminating; NNRTI allosteric — one mutation kills the class; lenacapavir capsid) · integration (INSTI) · maturation (PI — resistance uncommon). Cobicistat is not an antiretroviral.
  • Testing: Ag/Ab combo with p24 → antibody differentiation → NAT (positive = acute). Eclipse period day 0–10 detects nothing. Western blot obsolete.
  • CD4 stages; viral load transmits. AIDS = CD4 <200 (or <14%) OR an AIDS-defining OI. OI risk greatest <50. ALC <1,000 predicts CD4 <200.
  • Thresholds: <200 PJP/Cryptococcus/Candida · <100 toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing) · <50 CMV, Cryptococcus, MAC, CNS lymphoma.
  • PJP: cholesterol not ergosterol → TMP/SMX. Steroids if PaO₂ <70 or A–a ≥35. Start ART within 2 weeks.
  • IRIS: 10–20%, median 48 days, improving CD4/viral load with clinical worsening. Do not delay ART.
  • Prophylaxis: TMP/SMX <200 (PJP) and <100 (toxo). Live vaccines only if CD4 ≥ 200.
  • Boosters (ritonavir, cobicistat) inhibit CYP3A4 → OTC nasal steroid → iatrogenic Cushing.
  • U = U, CDC < 200 copies/mL. PARTNER trial: 74,000 episodes, zero transmissions. PrEP ~99% sexual; PEP within 72 hours.
Clotting · LO 9 · 40 · 46 · 47 · 49 · 70 · 84 · 85

Microangiopathies

  • All TMAs: PT, aPTT and fibrinogen normal. DIC: both prolonged, fibrinogen falling. Schistocytes in all — the panel is the discriminator.
  • TTP = ADAMTS13 deficient or IgG-inhibited → uncleaved ultra-large VWF multimers seize platelets → systemic, brain. Acquired form presents in the 20s–30s. Rx plasma exchange (replaces enzyme + removes antibody); no platelet transfusion. Pentad: fever, ↓plt, MAHA, neuro, renal — treat before all five.
  • HUS = Shiga toxin (E. coli O157:H7) → glomerular endothelium → kidney, bloody diarrhoea prodrome.
  • aHUS = unregulated alternative complement (factor H, factor I, MCP/CD46, thrombomodulin) → MAC destroys endothelium. Rx eculizumab. Genotype before transplant — liver-made regulator recurs, kidney-made one does not.

Thrombophilias

  • Virchow: endothelial damage · stasis · hypercoagulability. ~25% of everyone has a thrombophilia; ~60% of DVT patients do.
  • Lose a brake (antithrombin, protein C, protein S) → RR 15–19×. Push the accelerator (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) → RR 3–5×.
  • FVL R506Q, 5% of Caucasians, 20–30% of VTE — activated protein C resistance. G20210A is a 3′ UTR mutation raising mRNA stability: normal protein, more of it.
  • Antithrombin: homozygous lethal; lost in proteinuria, chest tubes → heparin resistance. Homozygous protein C/S → neonatal purpura fulminans.
  • Lupus anticoagulant = double misnomer. Mix fails to correct; extra phospholipid corrects. Anti-cardiolipin → false-positive syphilis test. Needs a clinical criterion plus persistence 12 weeks apart. Antibody without the syndrome is not anticoagulated.

HIT & duration

  • HIT is prothrombotic. Days 5–14, >50% fall, venous:arterial 4:1. Anti-heparin/PF4 antibody, then SRA if it conflicts.
  • 4T: 6–8 treat, don't wait · 0–3 do not test · 4–5 test. Rx argatroban / lepirudin. Avoid: warfarin alone (gangrene), LMWH (cross-reacts), no anticoagulation.
  • Only a long heparin tail bridges antithrombin to thrombin → aPTT works for UFH (1.5–2.5×) but anti-Xa only for LMWH/fondaparinux.
  • Recurrence sets duration: major transient 3% · minor reversible 5% · unprovoked/persistent 10% in year one.
  • Test if: family history, <45 yrs, no risk factors, recurrent, unusual site. Heparin ↓antithrombin, warfarin ↓protein C/S, acute illness ↑factor 8 → wait months, off anticoagulation. Genetic testing any time, once.
Malignancy · LO 3 · 6 · 8 · 10 · 27 · 41 · 43 · 44 · 45 · 51 · 52 · 53 · 59 · 60 · 63 · 64 · 67 · 75 · 76 · 87 · 92

The core construct

  • Less differentiated → AGGRESSIVE. More differentiated → INDOLENT. Tempo follows the stage at transformation.
  • >20% blasts = acute leukemia (marrow OR blood). Same line: MDS vs AML, and CML blast phase.
  • Aggressive lymphoma is CURABLE; indolent is not — chemo kills dividing cells. A third of follicular patients are never treated.
  • Emergencies: DIC (low fibrinogen, long PT/PTT, schistocytes — APL) and tumour lysis (K, PO4, urate UP, Ca DOWN).

Myeloid

  • APL: t(15;17) → PML-RARA → ATRA on suspicion. DIC kills before cytogenetics return. 90% survival.
  • MDS: hypercellular marrow + cytopenias = ineffective production. Epigenetic → hypomethylating agents. 30% → AML, but 50% die of bleeding/infection.
  • CML: t(9;22) / BCR-ABL / Philadelphia. TKI → median 2–5 yr becomes 95% alive at 10 yr. T315I → ponatinib.
  • Accelerated = blasts 10–19% OR basophils ≥20%. Blast phase = >20% blasts. Read the cell type before the number.
  • CML vs leukemoid: BCR-ABL positive, basophilia, LOW leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (leukemoid = high LAP, toxic granulation, a trigger).
  • MPNs are JAK2-driven — danger is thrombosis. PV → phlebotomy (Hct <45 M / <42 F). ET → hydroxyurea. MF → pancytopenia; ruxolitinib helps symptoms + survival, NOT counts.

Lymphoid & plasma cell

  • ALL: commonest childhood cancer; lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, CNS distinguish it from AML. Children >90% → adults 30%.
  • CLL: CD5+, CD10−, CD20+, CD23+. vs mantle cell: CD23 NEGATIVE + t(11;14)/cyclin D1. 13q favourable; 17p/11q high risk; IgVH mutated = good.
  • DLBCL → R-CHOP. IPI 4–5 = 50%; double hit (MYC + BCL2/BCL6) ≈ 30% — worse than the worst clinical score. Burkitt t(8;14).
  • Gastric MALT → eradicate H. pylori and the lymphoma can resolve. Hepatitis C → nodal MZL.
  • Hodgkin: bimodal 15–35 / >55; 50% EBV; EXCISIONAL biopsy; stage with PET/CT + ESR; alcohol-induced nodal pain, pruritus, eosinophilia. ABVD.
  • Waldenström = IgM pentamer → hyperviscosity (emergent plasmapheresis), neuropathy, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins, bleeding. MYD88.
  • Myeloma: damage from the product. Light chains → renal failure even with a small spike. CRAB. MGUS <10% & <3 g/dL (1%/yr); smoldering 10–60% or ≥3 g/dL (10%/yr for 5 yr). Neither is treated.
Antineoplastics · LO 17 · 18 · 21 · 22 · 57

Principles

  • Four classes: cytotoxic (dividing cells) · targeted (follows the target) · immuno (autoimmunity) · hormonal (hormone withdrawal).
  • Neoadjuvant = before surgery; adjuvant = after. Log kill = constant FRACTION, so cycles are mathematically necessary. 10⁹ cells ≈ 1 g = detection threshold.
  • Combine drugs with different mechanisms AND different organ toxicity — shared toxicity forces dose reduction.
  • Rescue: leucovorin↔methotrexate (but ENHANCES 5-FU) · mesna↔acrolein · dexrazoxane↔anthracycline.
  • Resistance: DNA repair (alkylators/cisplatin) · trapping (bleomycin, cisplatin, anthracyclines) · altered DHFR (methotrexate) · failed prodrug activation (antimetabolites) · MDR1/P-glycoprotein efflux → cross-resistance to unrelated drugs · sanctuary (CNS, testes).
  • G0 cells resist CCS drugs — which is why CCNS alkylators/platinums/anthracyclines are the backbone.

Chemo Man — the six pairings

  • Cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide → haemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein; mesna)
  • Bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis (marrow SPARED)
  • Cisplatin → oto- + nephrotoxicity + vomiting; carboplatin trades these for myelosuppression; oxaliplatin → COLD-induced neuropathy
  • Doxorubicin/daunorubicin/trastuzumab → cardiotoxicity (lifetime cumulative cap)
  • Oxaliplatin/vincristine/taxanes → peripheral neuropathy
  • Irinotecan → potentially fatal diarrhoea (atropine early, loperamide late)
  • Also: vincristine NEVER intrathecal (fatal). vinCRIStine → nerves; vinBLAStine → marrow. Cytarabine → cerebellar ataxia + conjunctivitis. Procarbazine is an MAO inhibitor.
  • Support: epoetin (RBC) · filgrastim (neutrophils) · sargramostim · plerixafor (mobilisation) · -opag/-ostim (platelets). -setron = 5-HT3; -pitant = NK1.

Targeted, immuno & hormonal

  • Size decides site: antibodies (~145 kDa) act outside the cell; small molecules go inside. No mAbs among signal-transduction inhibitors.
  • Small molecule → CYP3A4 interactions, food effects, QT prolongation, diarrhoea, raised LFTs. Antibody → infusion reactions + on-target toxicity (EGFR → acne-like rash).
  • Trastuzumab → heart failure (HER2 on cardiomyocytes). Daratumumab (CD38) interferes with cross-match — warn the blood bank.
  • ADC: the second word is the payload. -emtansine/-vedotin = anti-microtubule (neuropathy); -deruxtecan/-govitecan = topoisomerase (myelosuppression).
  • Checkpoints: CTLA-4 = ipilimumab · PD-1 = pembrolizumab/nivolumab · PD-L1 = atezolizumab, avelumab, durvalumab · LAG-3 = relatlimab. Toxicity = any organ ending in -itis → treat with corticosteroids.
  • CRS (4–16 h, fever + hypotension + hypoxia) → tocilizumab. ICANS (day 3–9, confusion/seizure) → dexamethasone, NOT tocilizumab.
  • Hormonal: SERM = agonist in bone and endometrium (tamoxifen → endometrial cancer + clots, protects bone). Aromatase inhibitor removes estrogen everywhere → osteoporosis; postmenopausal only. GnRH agonist → tumour FLARE → cover with an anti-androgen. Abiraterone (CYP17) → hypokalaemia, give with prednisone.
Lymphatics & VTE · LO 9 · 15 · 24 · 56 · 72 · 90 · 91

Lymphatics

  • Primary function = return proteins and fluid to the blood. Lymph is protein-rich — which is why obstruction swells so persistently.
  • NEVER place a LEFT internal jugular line — the thoracic duct enters the posterior wall at the left subclavian/IJ confluence → chylothorax. Use right IJ, subclavian or femoral.
  • Node: cortex = B cells/follicles · paracortex = T cells · medulla = plasma cells. Antigen-INdependent maturation in marrow/thymus; antigen-DEPENDENT in nodes/spleen/mucosa.
  • Thymus: cortex → positive selection → medulla; non-responders apoptose. Involutes after puberty.
  • Peyer's patches (ileum) → IgA = “mucosal antiseptic paint”; tonsils → IgG/IgE, directly antigen-exposed and non-encapsulated. Ileocecal resection in a baby → loses IgA → translocation sepsis.
  • Lymphedema: square toes = Stemmer sign (cannot tent the web space). Unilateral + negative ultrasound + square toes. Developed world = iatrogenic; worldwide = filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti). Complication: lymphangiosarcoma.

DVT/PE — starting and stopping

  • DVT → Doppler ultrasound first, always. CTEPH → V/Q scan, not CT angiography.
  • Apixaban and Rivaroxaban go it alone (loading dose, no heparin). Dabigatran and Edoxaban need Days of heparin first.
  • DOAC preferred over warfarin — equal efficacy, LESS bleeding (especially intracranial). Except: pregnancy · massive clot · extremes of weight · gastric bypass · CrCl <30 · HIT · splanchnic · antiphospholipid syndrome (evidence of HARM) · enzyme inducers.
  • Duration: provoked = 3 months, then stop. Unprovoked = at least 3 months then decide. Second unprovoked = long-term. Cancer = LMWH ≥3 months.
  • Fatal recurrence 0.3–1%/yr vs fatal bleeding 0.2–0.6%/yr — overlapping, hence “suggest” and Grade 2B.
  • AMPLIFY-EXTEND: apixaban 2.5 mg = full benefit, placebo-level bleeding. EINSTEIN-CHOICE: aspirin is markedly inferior and not safer.
  • VTE-BLEED ≥2 = high risk (13%); active cancer alone scores 2. IVC filter: one solid indication — absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; it increases recurrent DVT.
